item.title: About This Resource & How We Research
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
This resource helps people find the official legal status of keeping, breeding, selling, and transporting a domesticated roof rat (Rattus rattus) wherever they live, and what to do about it.

Legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.

What this is, and is not

It is a research aid built from official government sources. It is not legal advice, and we are not lawyers. Laws change, and local officials interpret them in ways we cannot control. Always read the official source yourself and, when it matters, confirm directly with the agency before you act.

How we research each jurisdiction

  • We start from official primary sources: statutes, regulations, and the responsible agencies (wildlife, agriculture, customs).
  • We use structured deep research, then verify every claim against the official source and link it.
  • Where the published rules are unclear, we say so, and where possible we confirm directly with the agency in writing.
  • Every answer carries a confidence level and a last-verified date. Pages we have not yet agency-confirmed are marked preliminary.

What the labels mean

LegalAllowed, with no special permit.
Legal with a permitAllowed, but a permit, license, or registration is required.
RestrictedAllowed only under specific conditions or limits.
ProhibitedNot allowed.
Unregulated / unclearNo rule found, or the law is silent or ambiguous.
Not yet researchedNot yet researched. Here is how you can help.

Species, not domestication

An important nuance: most laws regulate a species, not whether your animals are tame. A domesticated roof rat is still Rattus rattus. So an exemption for “domestic” animals (which often means only Rattus norvegicus (the fancy rat)) may or may not cover a roof rat. We flag this wherever it matters, and it is often the heart of the advocacy case for fairer rules.

Help us keep it accurate

Found something out of date, or know the rule for your area? Please tell us, ideally with a link to the official source, and we will verify and update. This resource gets better with every contribution.

item.title: How to Find Your Local Law (Step by Step)
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Can’t find your area in our guide yet? Here is exactly how to get the official answer for where you live, the same way we do it. It usually takes a few emails.

Legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.

Step 1: Know the exact animal

The pet roof rat is Rattus rattus. When you contact an agency, use the scientific name and make clear the animals are captive-bred and kept as pets, not wild-caught. (also relevant: it is a different species from Rattus norvegicus, the fancy rat). Many rules that exempt “domestic” animals mean only that other species, so do not assume.

Step 2: Identify your jurisdiction(s)

Rules can stack at three levels: your country, your state or region, and your city or county. Check all three; a permissive country can still have a local ban, and vice versa.

Instant tool: check your city or county ordinance

The local layer is the hardest to research, because most city and county animal ordinances live in databases that are not indexed well by ordinary search. This finder builds targeted searches of the major municipal-code libraries for your area, scoped to the words that matter.

Instant city / county ordinance finder

Local rules are the hardest layer to find. Type your city or region, and this builds ready-made searches of the major municipal-code libraries (Municode, American Legal Publishing, eCode360) plus a plain web search, for the words that matter. It opens an ordinary web search in a new tab; nothing is sent to us.

Once you are in your code, search these terms: rodent, exotic animal, wild animal, prohibited animal, number of pets / pet limit. Found your rule? Tell us and we will add your city.

Step 3: Ask the right agencies

  • Wildlife agency: non-native and captive-wildlife rules, a common place a non-traditional pet is regulated.
  • Agriculture / animal-health department: sale, dealer licensing, and import health certificates.
  • Customs / border or import authority: bringing animals across borders.
  • Local animal control or city clerk: city and county ordinances.

Step 4: Ask the questions, in writing

Email each agency and ask, specifically, about a roof rat kept as a pet:

  • Is it legal to keep one as a pet? Any permit or registration?
  • Is it legal to breed them? Any license?
  • Is it legal to sell or give them to others? Any dealer license?
  • What is required to transport or import them (health certificate, permit)?

Ask for the answer in writing and for the specific statute or rule, so you have a record and a citation. Write to the agency in the official language of your country.

Step 5: Get it in writing, and share it

Save the agency’s reply. Then please send it to us with the source links so we can verify it and add your area to the guide, helping the next person who asks.

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in United Arab Emirates? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin

Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United Arab Emirates

Summary. The UAE is now AGENCY-CONFIRMED PROHIBITED for private roof rats, and it is a textbook species-not-domestication case. The Ministry of Climate Change and Environment (MOCCAE) confirmed in writing (June 2026) that the 'domesticated rats' exemption to the rodent-keeping restriction under Federal Law No. 22 of 2016 applies STRICTLY to the fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus). Because the roof rat (R. rattus) is not classified as a domesticated pet under UAE regulations, private individuals may not keep, breed, possess, or import it; the only import pathway is for licensed research entities or zoological facilities. (An earlier reading that the exemption might cover domesticated R. rattus is closed by MOCCAE's species-specific reply.)

Key points here are confirmed in writing by the responsible agency (see below).
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
Confirmed by the agencies.
  • UAE Ministry of Climate Change and Environment (MOCCAE), written reply June 2026: the 'domesticated rats' exemption to the rodent-keeping restriction under Federal Law No. 22 of 2016 applies STRICTLY to the fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus). The roof rat (Rattus rattus) is not classified as a domesticated pet under UAE regulations, so private individuals may not keep, breed, possess, or import it; importation is restricted to licensed research entities or zoological facilities.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

MOCCAE confirmed in writing (June 2026) that the 'domesticated rats' exemption under Federal Law No. 22 of 2016 applies STRICTLY to the fancy rat (R. norvegicus); the roof rat (R. rattus) is not classified as a domesticated pet under UAE regulations, so private individuals may not keep it. A textbook species-not-domestication prohibition.

Sources: UAE Federal Legislation Portal, Official UAE Government Portal

Breeding   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

Prohibited for private individuals: MOCCAE (June 2026) confirmed R. rattus may not be kept, bred, or possessed privately; only the fancy rat is within the exemption.

Sources: MOCCAE, UAE Federal Legislation Portal

Selling or giving away   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

Prohibited for private individuals: since R. rattus may not be privately kept/bred/possessed (MOCCAE, June 2026), private sale or transfer is not permitted either.

Sources: UAE Federal Legislation Portal, MOCCAE

Transport & import   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

Import is prohibited for private individuals (MOCCAE, June 2026): there is no private-owner import permit pathway for R. rattus; importation is restricted strictly to licensed research entities or zoological facilities. Never release.

Sources: MOCCAE, MOCCAE (mirrored)

Restrictions & responsibilities

Keeping a domesticated roof rat is exempt from the UAE dangerous-animal ban (no keeper permit). Commercial breeding/selling needs a MOCCAE animal-care-activities licence + a local commercial licence; importing needs a MOCCAE live-animal import permit (AED 100) + the rodent veterinary health certificate. ⚠️ Confirm with MOCCAE that 'domesticated rats' in the Annex covers captive-bred R. rattus. Never release.
  • For import: apply for the MOCCAE live-animal import permit + obtain the rodent health certificate from the origin country
  • For commercial breeding/sale: MOCCAE animal-care-activities licence + local DED/municipal licence
  • Confirm R. rattus species-scope with MOCCAE

Forms: MOCCAE — Import Permit for Live Animals and Birds · Where: Ministry of Climate Change & Environment (MOCCAE) · Fees: Import permit AED 100

Source: MOCCAE, MOCCAE

It appears you can't currently keep a roof rat as a pet in United Arab Emirates. Please confirm with the official sources above before acting. If you'd like to see this change, you can contact your representatives and the responsible agencies, ask them to treat a domesticated Rattus rattus line fairly and tell us what you learn so we can help others.

Help change this

How to help in United Arab Emirates

The UAE bars private individuals from keeping most rodents but exempts 'domesticated rats'. MOCCAE has confirmed it reads that exemption to mean only the fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus). A captive-bred, domesticated roof rat (R. rattus) is therefore prohibited to keep, breed, or import, even though it is equally domesticated. This is a classification gap, not a safety judgment.

The ask: Ask MOCCAE to recognize captive-bred, multi-generation domesticated Rattus rattus as a 'domesticated rat' within the existing Federal Law No. 22 of 2016 exemption (the same exemption the fancy rat holds), or to set out a private-keeper pathway. The animals are tame, indoor-kept, and never released. The already-permitted fancy rat is itself the wild brown rat (R. norvegicus), domesticated only in the 19th century (see https://blonderoofrat.com/how-the-sewer-rat-became-the-fancy-rat/), so a captive-bred R. rattus is the same case one species over.

Where the lever really is: MOCCAE confirmed this is its classification under the regulation, so the lever is the agency/regulator. Ask MOCCAE to read the 'domesticated rats' exemption to include domesticated R. rattus, an interpretation or classification change. If MOCCAE states that only a regulatory amendment can do it, that points to the rule-making authority. It is not a courts matter.

Where to send it (more than one channel helps):

  • UAE Ministry of Climate Change and Environment (MOCCAE) (executive / agency) — info@moccae.gov.ae
    MOCCAE administers Federal Law No. 22 of 2016 and decides which rats count as 'domesticated'; it replies to written inquiries (verified, June 2026).

A starting-point message — please put it in your own words; a short personal note carries far more weight than an identical form letter:

English
To the Ministry of Climate Change and Environment,

Under Federal Law No. 22 of 2016, individuals may keep 'domesticated rats', but I understand the Ministry currently reads this to cover only the fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus), excluding the domesticated roof rat (Rattus rattus).

I respectfully ask the Ministry to recognize captive-bred, multi-generation domesticated Rattus rattus as a 'domesticated rat' within this exemption, the same way the fancy rat is treated. These animals are selectively bred for tameness over many generations, kept indoors as companion animals, and never released; they pose no greater risk than the fancy rat already permitted.

If recognition requires a regulatory step, I would be grateful to know the process. Thank you for your consideration.

[Your name]
العربية
إلى وزارة التغير المناخي والبيئة الموقرة،

بموجب القانون الاتحادي رقم 22 لسنة 2016، يُسمح للأفراد بتربية «الجرذان المستأنسة»، إلا أنني أتفهم أن الوزارة تفسّر ذلك حالياً على أنه يشمل فقط الجرذ النرويجي (Rattus norvegicus)، مع استثناء الجرذ الأسود المستأنس (Rattus rattus).

أرجو من الوزارة الكريمة الاعتراف بالجرذ الأسود (Rattus rattus) المربّى في الأسر عبر أجيال متعددة باعتباره «جرذاً مستأنساً» ضمن هذا الاستثناء، تماماً كما يُعامَل الجرذ النرويجي. فهذه الحيوانات تُنتخب للأُلفة عبر أجيال عديدة، وتُربّى داخل المنازل كحيوانات أليفة، ولا تُطلق في البيئة أبداً، وهي لا تشكّل خطراً أكبر من الجرذ النرويجي المسموح به بالفعل.

وإذا كان هذا الاعتراف يتطلب إجراءً تنظيمياً، فسأكون ممتناً لمعرفة الآلية. شكراً لكم على حسن اهتمامكم.

[الاسم]

Did you take action, or get a response? Tell us — it helps the next person, and we track what actually works.

Official sources

  • u.ae — Banning private ownership of dangerous animals (official summary) — Official UAE Government Portal
  • MOCCAE — Import Permit for Live Animals and Birds (AED 100, 90-day; rodents covered) — MOCCAE
  • MOCCAE — Veterinary Health Certificate model for exporting rodents/lagomorphs/reptiles to the UAE — MOCCAE (mirrored)
  • MOCCAE — License for Practicing Animal Care Activities (breeding/import-export) — MOCCAE

Search terms: Rattus rattus, الجرذ الأسود, roof rat, black rat.

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Argentina? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Argentina

Summary. Argentina classifies the roof rat (Rattus rattus) as a Category 1 Invasive Exotic Species (EEI-1, 'especie restringida y de control obligatorio') under Resolución 109/2021. Article 5 of that resolution imposes a blanket federal ban on the breeding (cría), purchase/sale, donation, release, importation, and inter-jurisdictional movement of EEI-1 species — so breeding, selling/giving, and transport of a roof rat are prohibited, with no lawful permit pathway (the Art. 5 ban preempts the otherwise-available fauna-operator registry of Res. 170/2021). Private possession ('tenencia') of a pre-existing captive-bred specimen sits in a deliberate gap: Art. 5 enumerates banned actions but omits passive possession, and the constitutional legality principle (Const. Nacional Art. 19) means no one can be deprived of what the law does not forbid — so keeping is best read as unregulated/unclear rather than expressly legal, and a province or municipality could still add a local ban. The brown/fancy rat (R. norvegicus) is taxonomically EEI-1 too, yet is sold and kept openly thanks to a de-facto domestication exemption — an exemption R. rattus, lacking any recognized domestic lineage, does not enjoy.

Key points here are confirmed in writing by the responsible agency (see below).
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
Confirmed by the agencies.
  • Dirección Nacional de Biodiversidad (rpuofs@jefatura.gob.ar), written reply 2026-06-11: 'Esta Dirección de Biodiversidad interviene solamente animales silvestres. Por la tenencia de un animal doméstico, consulte ante la autoridad jurisdiccional correspondiente al lugar donde se encuentre el ejemplar.' (This Biodiversity Directorate only intervenes for WILD animals; for the possession of a DOMESTIC animal, consult the provincial/jurisdictional authority where the specimen is located.) — the federal wildlife authority disclaims jurisdiction over the keeping (tenencia) of a domestic specimen, confirming that possession of a kept R. rattus is a provincial matter rather than a federal wild-fauna question.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-10

Art. 5 of Resolución 109/2021 enumerates the banned activities for EEI-1 species — cría, compra/venta, donación, liberación, introducción al territorio nacional, and movimiento interjurisdiccional — but conspicuously omits 'tenencia' (passive private possession). Under the constitutional legality principle (Const. Nacional Art. 19: no inhabitant may be deprived of what the law does not forbid), merely keeping a pre-existing captive-bred R. rattus indoors is not an enumerated federal offense, so federal authorities have no Art. 5 mandate to confiscate it. This is a jurisprudential gap, not an affirmative protected right: provinces and municipalities retain the police power to enact stricter local bans on keeping invasive rodents, and federal silence does not equal permission. Treat as unregulated/unclear — neither expressly authorized nor expressly prohibited.

Sources: Ministerio de Ambiente y Desarrollo Sostenible (vía Infoleg), Ministerio de Ambiente y Desarrollo Sostenible (vía Infoleg), Honorable Congreso de la Nación Argentina (vía Infoleg), Constitución de la Nación Argentina (vía Infoleg), Sistema de Información de Biodiversidad / APN

Breeding   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

Art. 5 of Resolución 109/2021 expressly prohibits 'su cría o cultivo' for EEI-1 species in places under national jurisdiction, with no hobbyist or small-breeder threshold. Because R. rattus is EEI-1, the Dirección Nacional de Biodiversidad is legally stripped of authority to grant any breeding license, and the Art. 5 ban preempts the fauna-operator registry (RPUOFS, Res. 170/2021) — so even a fully compliant criadero application would be administratively dead on arrival. There is no lawful private or commercial pathway to breed the species; any breeding is treated as an illicit act of wildlife trafficking. (By contrast, R. norvegicus is bred openly under a de-facto domestication exemption that R. rattus does not share.)

Sources: Ministerio de Ambiente y Desarrollo Sostenible (vía Infoleg), Ministerio de Ambiente y Desarrollo Sostenible (vía Infoleg), Ministerio de Ambiente y Desarrollo Sostenible (vía Infoleg), Honorable Congreso de la Nación Argentina (vía Infoleg)

Selling or giving away   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

Art. 5 of Resolución 109/2021 expressly prohibits 'compra y venta, donación' of EEI-1 species — covering both sale and non-commercial gifting/donation. There is no lawful avenue to commercialize or transfer R. rattus: the Art. 5 ban preempts the fauna-operator registry (Res. 170/2021), so no dealer/criadero license can issue, and even gifting is enumerated as a banned act. This forecloses any private give-away as well as commercial sale. (R. norvegicus is sold openly only because of an uncodified de-facto domestication exemption that R. rattus does not formally enjoy.)

Sources: Ministerio de Ambiente y Desarrollo Sostenible (vía Infoleg), Ministerio de Ambiente y Desarrollo Sostenible (vía Infoleg), Ministerio de Ambiente y Desarrollo Sostenible (vía Infoleg), Honorable Congreso de la Nación Argentina (vía Infoleg)

Transport & import   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

Art. 5 of Resolución 109/2021 imposes a blanket ban on 'la introducción al territorio nacional y el movimiento interjurisdiccional' of EEI-1 species, so both importing R. rattus and moving it across provincial lines are prohibited. On import, the SENASA sanitary pathway (CVI, TAD, SIGTrámites) is entirely subordinate to the environmental veto: the Dirección Nacional de Biodiversidad must authorize a wildlife import first (Decreto 666/1997 Art. 22 empowers it to reject ecologically harmful imports), and for an EEI-1 species it is obligated to refuse — so SENASA can never issue the final entry permit. Internally, provincial fauna authorities cannot issue a transit guide (guía de tránsito) for a federally restricted EEI-1 species for personal relocation, leaving the animal legally trapped in its current province. No lawful transport pathway exists. (Intra-provincial movement within a single jurisdiction is not reached by the inter-jurisdictional ban, but the keep status governs there.)

Sources: Ministerio de Ambiente y Desarrollo Sostenible (vía Infoleg), Ministerio de Ambiente y Desarrollo Sostenible (vía Infoleg), Poder Ejecutivo Nacional (Argentina.gob.ar), SENASA (Servicio Nacional de Sanidad y Calidad Agroalimentaria), Honorable Congreso de la Nación Argentina (vía Infoleg)

Restrictions & responsibilities

Because R. rattus is a Category 1 Invasive Exotic Species (EEI-1), Art. 5 of Resolución 109/2021 bans breeding (cría), purchase/sale, donation, release (liberación), importation, and inter-jurisdictional movement, with no lawful permit pathway — the EEI-1 status strips the wildlife directorate of authority to license the species and preempts the fauna-operator registry (Res. 170/2021). Passive private possession ('tenencia') is not on the Art. 5 ban list, but a possessor is then locked in: cannot lawfully breed it, give it away, sell its offspring, or move it across provinces. Provinces/municipalities may add stricter local bans. Never release — liberation is expressly prohibited.
  • Do NOT breed, sell, give away, import, or move R. rattus across provincial lines — these are banned for EEI-1 species (Res. 109/2021 Art. 5)
  • Never release a roof rat into the environment (liberación is expressly prohibited)
  • If advocating: ask the Dirección Nacional de Biodiversidad for a written clarification on tenencia and a possible Art. 6 exception extending R. norvegicus-style domestic treatment to captive-bred R. rattus

Where: Dirección Nacional de Biodiversidad (Subsecretaría de Ambiente) for clarifications/exceptions; SENASA for import questions; provincial fauna authority for transit

Source: Ministerio de Ambiente y Desarrollo Sostenible (vía Infoleg), Ministerio de Ambiente y Desarrollo Sostenible (vía Infoleg), Ministerio de Ambiente y Desarrollo Sostenible (vía Infoleg), Poder Ejecutivo Nacional (Argentina.gob.ar)

The rule here isn't settled yet. Use our step-by-step guide to confirm with your agencies and send us what you find.

Help change this

How to help in Argentina

In Argentina the roof rat (Rattus rattus) is listed as a Category 1 Invasive Exotic Species (EEI-1) under Resolución 109/2021. Article 5 of that resolution bans the breeding, sale, donation, release, import, and inter-jurisdictional movement of EEI-1 species. Because the species is EEI-1, the Dirección Nacional de Biodiversidad has no authority to issue a breeder/operator license for it, so the otherwise-available fauna-operator registry (Res. 170/2021) is foreclosed. The common fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus) carries the identical EEI-1 listing, yet it is bred, transported, and sold openly nationwide because authorities treat its laboratory and fancy strains as domestic animals (animales domésticos) outside the wildlife regime. The fancy rat is itself the wild brown rat, domesticated only in the 19th century; R. rattus never received the same institutional recognition, so a tame, captive-bred roof rat is subject to the full invasive-wildlife prohibitions on the basis of its species name. Separately, private possession ('tenencia') is absent from the Art. 5 ban list, leaving an owner in a gray zone: not prosecuted for keeping the animal, but unable to lawfully breed, give, sell, or move it.

The ask: Ask the Dirección Nacional de Biodiversidad to confirm in writing (a) that passive private possession of a pre-existing captive-bred Rattus rattus, kept indoors and never released, is not among the activities banned by Art. 5 of Resolución 109/2021; and (b) whether a formal regulatory exception exists or can be granted, via Art. 6 of Res. 109/2021, an internal dictamen, or administrative jurisprudence, that extends to captive-bred, closed-colony R. rattus the same de-facto domestic-animal treatment already afforded to R. norvegicus, so that documented captive-bred specimens fall outside the EEI-1 commercialization and transport prohibitions. Domestication, not wild ancestry, is what makes an animal a domestic companion: the dog descends from the wolf and the cat from a wild felid, yet both are recognized as domestic. The fancy rat (R. norvegicus) is itself the wild brown rat, domesticated only in the 19th century (see https://blonderoofrat.com/how-the-sewer-rat-became-the-fancy-rat/), so a multi-generation captive-bred R. rattus is domesticated on identical terms, one species over. The question is whether the agency will extend to R. rattus the domestic recognition it already applies to its near-twin. For anyone importing, ask SENASA whether an EEI-1-classified companion rodent is automatically rejected in the TAD system, or whether a Certificado Veterinario Internacional can be processed for a non-commercial captive-bred specimen with a biosecurity plan.

Where the lever really is: Lever: the agency (Dirección Nacional de Biodiversidad), not the legislature. No statute names or bans R. rattus by species; the prohibition flows from an administrative classification (EEI-1 under Resolución 109/2021, a Ministerio de Ambiente resolution) and its Art. 5 operative ban. Because the barrier is the agency's own classification and the absence of a formal domestication/captive-bred exception, the fix is administrative: Art. 6 of Res. 109/2021 contemplates regulated exceptions, and the directorate already exercises de-facto interpretive discretion by treating R. norvegicus as domestic. There is no hostile statute to repeal and nothing to take to Congress. Federal-vs-provincial dimension: the federal government controls inter-provincial commerce, imports, and the EEI list, but the police power over the contents of a private home falls to provinces and municipalities, so even a favorable national clarification on tenencia would not bind a province that enacts a stricter local ban. This is a federal-first ask whose protection is reinforced, not replaced, by keeping breeder and captive-origin paperwork.

Where to send it (more than one channel helps):

  • Dirección Nacional de Biodiversidad (Subsecretaría de Ambiente, Ministerio de Ambiente y Desarrollo Sostenible) (executive / agency) — rpuofs@jefatura.gob.ar
    The national environmental Application Authority that maintains the EEI list (Res. 109/2021), enforces the Art. 5 prohibitions, runs the fauna-operator registry (RPUOFS, Res. 170/2021), and holds the pre-import authorization power over wildlife. It is the only office that can issue a written clarification on tenencia and grant or interpret an Art. 6 exception extending captive-bred R. rattus the de-facto domestic treatment already given to R. norvegicus. rpuofs@ambiente.gob.ar is the directorate's wildlife-operator inbox; mesadeentradas@ambiente.gob.ar is the general entry desk. [Updated 2026-06-11: contact via rpuofs@jefatura.gob.ar after the directorate's 2026-04-01 migration from @ambiente.gob.ar; mesadeentradas@ambiente.gob.ar is dead (hard-bounce).]
  • SENASA — Dirección de Comercio Exterior Animal (Mascotas No Tradicionales) (executive / agency) — responde@senasa.gob.ar
    The national animal-health service that runs the import protocol for non-traditional pets (CVI, SIGTrámites/TAD). Sanitary clearance is subordinate to the environmental veto, so SENASA is the right office to ask whether an EEI-1 companion rodent is auto-rejected in TAD or whether a CVI can be processed for a non-commercial captive-bred specimen. responde@senasa.gob.ar is the confirmed general inbox; dcea@senasa.gob.ar reaches the foreign-animal-trade directorate.

A starting-point message — please put it in your own words; a short personal note carries far more weight than an identical form letter:

English
To the Dirección Nacional de Biodiversidad (Subsecretaría de Ambiente):

I am writing regarding the regulatory status of the roof rat (Rattus rattus) kept as an indoor companion animal. The species is listed as a Category 1 Invasive Exotic Species (EEI-1) under Resolución 109/2021, and Article 5 prohibits its breeding, sale, donation, release, import, and inter-jurisdictional movement.

I have two questions.

First, on possession (tenencia): Article 5 enumerates the banned activities but does not include passive private possession. Could you confirm in writing that keeping a pre-existing, captive-bred R. rattus indoors, never released into the environment, is not among the activities prohibited by Article 5?

Second, on parity with the fancy rat: Rattus norvegicus carries the identical EEI-1 listing, yet its captive-bred laboratory and fancy strains are bred, transported, and sold openly nationwide because they are treated in practice as domestic animals (animales domésticos) outside the wildlife regime. Domestication, not wild ancestry, is what makes an animal a domestic companion: the dog descends from the wolf and the cat from a wild felid, yet both are recognized as domestic. The fancy rat is itself the wild brown rat, domesticated only in the 19th century. A captive-bred R. rattus is, in every practical husbandry sense, indistinguishable from the fancy rat and equally non-releasable, domesticated on identical terms. Does any formal regulatory exception exist, via Article 6 of Resolución 109/2021, an internal dictamen, or administrative jurisprudence, that could extend to documented, closed-colony, captive-bred R. rattus the same domestic-animal treatment already afforded de facto to R. norvegicus, so that such specimens fall outside the EEI-1 commercialization and transport prohibitions?

I am asking to understand the regulatory framework and to keep any animal lawfully. Thank you for your time and guidance.

[Your name]
[Your contact details]
Español
A la Dirección Nacional de Biodiversidad (Subsecretaría de Ambiente):

Me dirijo a ustedes respecto de la situación regulatoria de la rata de techo (Rattus rattus) tenida como animal de compañía dentro del hogar. La especie está clasificada como Especie Exótica Invasora Categoría 1 (EEI-1) en el Anexo I de la Resolución 109/2021, y su Artículo 5 prohíbe su cría, compra y venta, donación, liberación, introducción al territorio nacional y movimiento interjurisdiccional.

Formulo dos consultas.

Primero, sobre la tenencia: el Artículo 5 enumera las actividades prohibidas pero no incluye la tenencia particular pasiva. ¿Podrían confirmarme por escrito que la tenencia de un ejemplar de R. rattus ya existente, nacido en cautiverio y mantenido íntegramente dentro de la vivienda, sin liberación al ambiente, no se encuentra entre las actividades prohibidas por el Artículo 5?

Segundo, sobre la paridad con la rata doméstica común: Rattus norvegicus figura con idéntica clasificación EEI-1, y sin embargo sus cepas de laboratorio y domésticas criadas en cautiverio se crían, transportan y venden abiertamente en todo el país porque en la práctica se las trata como animales domésticos fuera del régimen de fauna silvestre. La domesticación, y no el origen silvestre, es lo que hace de un animal un animal de compañía doméstico: el perro desciende del lobo y el gato de un félido silvestre, y aun así ambos son reconocidos como animales domésticos. La rata 'fancy' es la propia rata parda silvestre, domesticada apenas en el siglo XIX. Un ejemplar de R. rattus nacido y criado en cautiverio es, en todo sentido práctico de manejo, indistinguible de la rata 'fancy' e igualmente no liberable, domesticado en idénticos términos. ¿Existe alguna excepción reglamentaria formal, vía Artículo 6 de la Resolución 109/2021, un dictamen interno o jurisprudencia administrativa, que pueda extender a los ejemplares documentados de R. rattus, de colonia cerrada y criados en cautiverio, el mismo tratamiento de 'animal doméstico' que de hecho ya se otorga a R. norvegicus, de modo que tales ejemplares queden fuera de las prohibiciones de comercialización y transporte propias de la categoría EEI-1?

Mi consulta tiene por fin comprender el marco regulatorio y poder tener cualquier animal de manera lícita. Agradezco su tiempo y orientación.

[Su nombre]
[Sus datos de contacto]

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Australia? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Australia

Summary. Australia is far more open to keeping a roof rat as a pet than its 'invasive pest' reputation suggests, but with one hard federal wall. Live rodents cannot be imported into Australia as pets: R. rattus is not on the EPBC Act Live Import List and the Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry (DAFF) confirmed in writing (June 2026) there is no pathway to import one as a companion animal (live rats enter only for laboratory purposes). Domestic keeping, breeding and sale are regulated by the states and territories, and on the actual statutory lists the captive-bred roof rat is treated the same as the common fancy rat (R. norvegicus): legal and permit-free in most jurisdictions. The state pest schemes target free-living rats, not contained pets. Queensland's Biosecurity Act 2014 (Sch 1 Pt 4) names 'black rat (Rattus rattus)' and 'sewer rat (Rattus norvegicus)' as exceptions to the prohibited-invasive-animal list; Victoria's prohibited-pest gazette bans the Muridae family 'except Mus musculus, Rattus norvegicus, Rattus rattus'; NSW puts both rats and the house mouse in the Biosecurity Act 2015 Schedule 3 carve-out (the 'animals to which Part does not apply' division), leaving them permitted subject only to the General Biosecurity Duty; South Australia's declared-animals list defines a Class 4 'Black rat (domestic)' (bred and kept in captivity) to which the keeping prohibition does not apply; Western Australia's Organism List records R. rattus as 'Permitted - s11 (Exempt)', identical to the brown rat; the Northern Territory lists 'Rat (laboratory strain) - Rattus rattus' as an animal that needs no wildlife permit; and the ACT's current pest-animal declaration does not list either rat species at all. Tasmania is the one practical hurdle: the roof rat is a 'Controlled animal' that needs an import permit to cross into the state, but once lawfully there, keeping requirements are nil. Everywhere the binding obligations are the same: keep the rat securely contained and never release it into the wild.

Key points here are confirmed in writing by the responsible agency (see below).
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
Confirmed by the agencies.
  • Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry (DAFF), Animal & Biological Imports Branch, written reply June 2026 (officer 'Mel'): live rats may be imported into Australia for laboratory purposes only; there are NO import conditions allowing rats as household pets, and 'there is currently no pathway to import Rattus rattus as a pet into Australia' (it is an introduced pest and not on the DCCEEW Live Import List). DAFF also confirmed that keeping, breeding, sale, and movement WITHIN Australia, and pest-species management, are regulated by STATE/TERRITORY governments - contact the relevant state/territory authority for those.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-14

Across all eight states and territories the captive-bred roof rat is lawful to keep with no specific keeping permit, on the same footing as the fancy rat. QLD Biosecurity Act 2014 Schedule 1 Part 4 makes 'All amphibians, mammals and reptiles other than the following' prohibited matter, and the 'following' (exceptions) list expressly includes 'black rat (Rattus rattus)' and 'sewer rat (Rattus norvegicus)', so neither is prohibited. VIC Gazette S399 (under the Catchment and Land Protection Act 1994) declares Schedule 1 prohibited pest animals as 'All species of Family Muridae that did not occur naturally in the wild in Australia before European settlement' but adds 'except Mus musculus, Rattus norvegicus, Rattus rattus'. NSW Biosecurity Act 2015 Schedule 3 places Mus musculus, Rattus norvegicus and Rattus rattus in 'Division 2 Animals to which Part does not apply' (with dog, cat, guinea pig, sheep, pig), not in the Part 3 section 4 prohibited-dealings list (which does name Rattus exulans, the Pacific rat), so keeping is permitted subject to the General Biosecurity Duty (secure containment, no release). SA's declared-animals list (Landscape South Australia Act 2019) defines Class 4 'Rattus rattus: Black rat (domestic) - meaning black rat(s) bred and kept in captivity (ie. held in a building or enclosure with security measures designed to ensure that the animal cannot escape...)', with only sections 189 and 191(1) applied, so the keeping/possession prohibition (s187), which applies to the wild form in Class 17, does not apply. WA's Organism List records 'rattus rattus... Permitted - s11 (Exempt)' (keeping category Exempt), identical to R. norvegicus. The NT lists 'Rat (laboratory strain) - Rattus rattus' as an animal that does not need a wildlife permit. The current ACT Pest Plants and Animals (Pest Animals) Declaration 2021 lists neither rat species. General animal-welfare law (state Prevention of Cruelty to Animals / Animal Welfare Acts) applies as it would to any pet.

Sources: Queensland Legislation (Office of the Queensland Parliamentary Counsel) / Biosecurity Queensland, Victorian Government Printer / Agriculture Victoria, NSW Legislation / NSW Department of Primary Industries, South Australian Government Gazette / PIRSA - Biosecurity SA, WA Department of Primary Industries and Regional Development (DPIRD) - Biosecurity and Agriculture Management Act 2007, Northern Territory Government - Dept of Environment, Parks and Water Security (DEPWS), ACT Legislation Register / ACT Environment, Planning and Sustainable Development Directorate (EPSDD)

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-14

Because the captive-bred roof rat is exempt from (or excepted out of) the prohibited-pest schedules in every jurisdiction, breeding it as a hobby needs no biosecurity or 'dealer' permit, exactly as for the fancy rat. The QLD exception, VIC Muridae exception, NSW Schedule 3 Division 2 carve-out, SA Class 4 'domestic' definition, WA 'Permitted - s11 (Exempt)' status, NT permit-exemption and ACT non-listing all attach to the species/animal, not to a particular activity, so breeding is permitted on the same basis as keeping. A private hobbyist breeding roof rats sits in the same legal space as someone breeding fancy mice or guinea pigs. The only overlays are general: animal-welfare law, and, if breeding becomes a commercial pet-shop or large-scale operation, state pet-shop / companion-animal codes of practice for rodents (which do not distinguish R. norvegicus from R. rattus).

Sources: Queensland Legislation (Office of the Queensland Parliamentary Counsel) / Biosecurity Queensland, Victorian Government Printer / Agriculture Victoria, NSW Legislation / NSW Department of Primary Industries, South Australian Government Gazette / PIRSA - Biosecurity SA, WA Department of Primary Industries and Regional Development (DPIRD) - Biosecurity and Agriculture Management Act 2007, Northern Territory Government - Dept of Environment, Parks and Water Security (DEPWS)

Selling or giving away   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-14

Selling or giving away a captive-bred roof rat is lawful wherever keeping it is lawful, with no biosecurity dealer licence required, because the species is carved out of the prohibited schedules (QLD exception list; VIC 'except... Rattus rattus'; NSW Schedule 3 Division 2; SA Class 4 'domestic'; WA Permitted - s11; NT permit-exempt; ACT not listed). A 'dealing' in the NSW sense (which includes selling, buying, breeding and disposing) is permitted for animals in the Division 2 carve-out subject to the General Biosecurity Duty. Private hobbyist transfer of either rat species is effectively unregulated by primary-industries departments. Commercial retail sale brings the business under state pet-shop codes of practice for rodents (welfare, enclosure, point-of-sale standards) and general consumer/animal-welfare law, but those apply equally to fancy rats. No jurisdiction bars the free or paid transfer of a domestic roof rat.

Sources: Queensland Legislation (Office of the Queensland Parliamentary Counsel) / Biosecurity Queensland, Victorian Government Printer / Agriculture Victoria, NSW Legislation / NSW Department of Primary Industries, South Australian Government Gazette / PIRSA - Biosecurity SA, WA Department of Primary Industries and Regional Development (DPIRD) - Biosecurity and Agriculture Management Act 2007, Northern Territory Government - Dept of Environment, Parks and Water Security (DEPWS)

Transport & import   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-14

This record encodes the INTERNATIONAL import position, which is the binding hard rule. AGENCY-CONFIRMED (DAFF, June 2026, Animal & Biological Imports Branch): there is currently no pathway to import Rattus rattus into Australia as a pet. Live rats may be imported for laboratory purposes only; R. rattus is an introduced pest, has no biosecurity import conditions as a companion animal, and is not on the EPBC Act Live Import List (a positive list, so a specimen not on it cannot be imported as a pet). Federal law: Biosecurity Act 2015 (Cth) + Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act 1999 (Live Import List, administered by DCCEEW; biosecurity import by DAFF). Within Australia, moving a lawfully held roof rat is generally unrestricted, with one exception: Tasmania classifies R. rattus as a 'Controlled animal' for which import into the state is permitted but requires an import permit (same controlled-animal/import-permit treatment as R. norvegicus). No advance permit applies to ordinary interstate movement on the mainland. Releasing the animal into the wild is prohibited everywhere.

Sources: Australian Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry (DAFF), Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water (DCCEEW), Biosecurity Tasmania / Dept of Natural Resources and Environment Tasmania (Nature Conservation Act 2002; Wildlife (General) Regulations 2010), Australian Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry (DAFF)

Restrictions & responsibilities

Tasmania import permit: the roof rat is a 'Controlled animal' in Tasmania. Bringing one into the state from interstate is permitted but requires an import permit from Biosecurity Tasmania (the same treatment as the brown/fancy rat). Once the animal is lawfully in Tasmania there is NO keeping or breeding permit requirement (the keeping column is nil). The permit step exists to protect Tasmania's offshore-island seabird ecosystems from escape.
  • Before moving a roof rat into Tasmania, apply to Biosecurity Tasmania (NRE Tas) Wildlife Management Branch for an import permit.
  • Expect to state the animal's origin and health status and to demonstrate secure, escape-proof housing.
  • After lawful import, no ongoing keeping/breeding licence or registration applies within Tasmania.
  • Confirm the current criteria with Biosecurity Tasmania, as the assessment standard for this species is not published in detail.

Forms: Requirements for importing and keeping wildlife in Tasmania (NRE Tas matrix) · Where: Biosecurity Tasmania, Department of Natural Resources and Environment Tasmania (NRE Tas). · Fees: Permit fee per Biosecurity Tasmania's current schedule (not published in the matrix; confirm with the agency).

Source: Biosecurity Tasmania / Dept of Natural Resources and Environment Tasmania (Nature Conservation Act 2002; Wildlife (General) Regulations 2010)

Secure containment and the duty not to release. Every state pest scheme that permits the captive roof rat conditions it on the animal being held so it cannot escape, and on never releasing it into the wild. SA's Class 4 'domestic' definition is literally 'bred and kept in captivity (ie. held in a building or enclosure with security measures designed to ensure that the animal cannot escape...)'; NSW's General Biosecurity Duty requires reasonable measures to prevent escape and release; release of a declared/invasive animal is an offence (e.g. SA Landscape South Australia Act s189). A roof rat that escapes or is released loses its protected 'domestic' status and becomes a wild pest subject to control.
  • House the rat in an escape-proof enclosure indoors.
  • Never release a roof rat into the wild, and rehome only to another lawful keeper.
  • If keeping a wild-type (agouti) animal, retain evidence it is captive-bred, since the 'domestic'/'laboratory strain' wording in SA, NT and the ACT distinguishes it from wild-caught rats.

Source: South Australian Government Gazette / PIRSA - Biosecurity SA, NSW Legislation / NSW Department of Primary Industries

International import is closed. Neither R. rattus nor R. norvegicus is on the EPBC Act Live Import List, so a pet rat of either species cannot be imported into Australia from overseas; DAFF confirmed live rats enter only for laboratory purposes. Lawful pet roof rats must come from captive stock already in Australia. There is no civilian permit pathway to import a pet roof rat internationally.
  • Do not attempt to import a pet roof rat from overseas; there is no lawful pathway.
  • Source any pet roof rat from existing captive-bred stock within Australia.
  • For any import question, contact DAFF (Animal & Biological Imports).

Where: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry (DAFF), Animal & Biological Imports Branch.

Source: Australian Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry (DAFF), Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water (DCCEEW)

Localised geographic control orders override the general permission. In specific vulnerable ecosystems R. rattus is targeted for mandatory eradication regardless of its general pet status, so possession there is barred. Example: the NSW Biosecurity (Rodent) Control Order targeting R. rattus and Mus musculus for eradication on Lord Howe Island; Tasmania and WA run island eradications (Big Green Island, Barrow Island, Penguin Island). These are place-specific, not a general taxonomic ban, but they are absolute within the declared zone.
  • If you live on or near an island or ecologically sensitive control zone, check for any local biosecurity control order before acquiring a roof rat.
  • Do not take a roof rat into a declared rodent-eradication area.

Where: Relevant state biosecurity authority / local control authority.

Source: NSW Legislation / NSW Department of Primary Industries

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Official sources

  • Biosecurity Act 2014 (Qld), Schedule 1 Part 4 (Invasive biosecurity matter - invasive animals): prohibits 'All amphibians, mammals and reptiles other than the following', and the exceptions list expressly includes 'black rat (Rattus rattus)' and 'sewer rat (Rattus norvegicus)' alongside cat, dog, guinea pig, house mouse. — Queensland Legislation (Office of the Queensland Parliamentary Counsel) / Biosecurity Queensland
  • Victoria Government Gazette No. S 399, 1 October 2010 (Catchment and Land Protection Act 1994): Schedule 1 Prohibited Pest Animals declares 'All species of Family Muridae that did not occur naturally in the wild in Australia before European settlement... except Mus musculus, Rattus norvegicus, Rattus rattus' (House Mouse, Brown Rat, Roof (Black) Rat excepted). — Victorian Government Printer / Agriculture Victoria
  • Biosecurity Act 2015 No 24 (NSW), Schedule 3 (Prohibited dealings - non-indigenous animals): Mus musculus, Rattus norvegicus (Brown rat) and Rattus rattus (Black rat) appear in 'Division 2 Animals to which Part does not apply' (with dog, cat, guinea pig, sheep, pig), NOT in the Part 3 s4 prohibited-dealings list (which names Rattus exulans, the Pacific rat). Permitted subject to the General Biosecurity Duty. — NSW Legislation / NSW Department of Primary Industries
  • South Australian Government Gazette No. 66, 26 September 2024 - List of Declared Animals (Landscape South Australia Act 2019): Class 4 'Rattus rattus: Black rat (domestic) - meaning black rat(s) bred and kept in captivity (ie. held in a building or enclosure with security measures designed to ensure that the animal cannot escape...)' and 'Rattus norvegicus: Brown Rat (domestic)' (provisions 189, 191(1) applied; keeping/possession prohibition s187 NOT applied). Class 17 covers the wild forms ('Mice and rats (wild)', provisions 187(1), 189). NOTE: wild form is Class 17, NOT 'Class 3' as the DR stated. — South Australian Government Gazette / PIRSA - Biosecurity SA
  • Western Australian Organism List (WAOL): 'rattus rattus' (Family Muridae, Black Rat) recorded as Legal Status 'Permitted - s11', Keeping category 'Exempt', Control category 'Unassigned', Present in WA - identical status to Rattus norvegicus (Brown/Norway Rat). 's11 Permitted' = may be kept without restriction once in WA (subject to interstate import requirements). — WA Department of Primary Industries and Regional Development (DPIRD) - Biosecurity and Agriculture Management Act 2007
  • Animals that do not need a permit (NT.GOV.AU): the mammals exemption list includes 'Rat (laboratory strain) - Rattus rattus' and 'Mouse (laboratory strain) - Mus musculus', so keeping a captive-bred specimen needs no NT wildlife permit. — Northern Territory Government - Dept of Environment, Parks and Water Security (DEPWS)
  • Pest Plants and Animals (Pest Animals) Declaration 2021 (DI2021-40 / notified instrument 2021-133) (ACT), under the Pest Plants and Animals Act 2005: the declared pest mammals are wild deer, Canis lupus (wild), Capra hircus (wild), Mustela putorius (wild), Oryctolagus cuniculus (wild), Sus scrofa (wild) and Vulpes vulpes - NEITHER Rattus rattus NOR Rattus norvegicus is listed, so a captive roof rat is not a declared pest in the ACT. (The DR cited an older 'proposed amendments' discussion paper with a 'Rattus rattus (wild)' line; the current instrument simply omits the species.) — ACT Legislation Register / ACT Environment, Planning and Sustainable Development Directorate (EPSDD)
  • Requirements for importing and keeping wildlife in Tasmania (NRE Tas matrix): 'Rat, Black (Ship Rat, House Rat) Rattus rattus' - Import Requirements: 'Controlled animal, import permitted, import permit required'; Requirements for Keeping: '-' (nil). 'Rat, Brown (Norwegian Rat) R. norvegicus' has the identical import-permit/nil-keeping treatment. — Biosecurity Tasmania / Dept of Natural Resources and Environment Tasmania (Nature Conservation Act 2002; Wildlife (General) Regulations 2010)
  • Live Import List (EPBC Act 1999) - DCCEEW: a positive list; a regulated live specimen not on the list cannot be imported (s303EK). Neither Rattus rattus nor Rattus norvegicus is listed for private pet import; exotic rodents are not importable as pets. — Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water (DCCEEW)

  • Importing cats and dogs and other pets - DAFF (general pet-import conditions; only a short approved set of pets can be imported, rodents not among them). — Australian Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry (DAFF)

item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Canada

Summary. Canada has no single national rule for keeping a roof rat — it is decided province by province, and the provinces diverge sharply. Alberta bans the entire genus Rattus outright (a famously 'rat-free' province); Saskatchewan explicitly lists the black rat on its captive-wildlife allowed list; Ontario, Quebec, and British Columbia all allow it (BC under a tame-captive exemption, Quebec with an import notice that the fancy rat is exempt from). Federally, the CFIA lets you import a pet rat with no permit or health certificate as long as it does NOT come from Africa. Check your province (below) AND your municipality.

Cross-checked against official government sources.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

The federal government does not regulate the day-to-day keeping of companion animals — that is left entirely to the provinces and municipalities, and the answer changes drastically at provincial borders. Alberta PROHIBITS keeping any rat (genus Rattus) with no pet exemption; Saskatchewan EXPLICITLY allows the black rat as captive wildlife; Ontario, Quebec, and British Columbia allow it. So there is no single Canadian answer — see your province below.

Sources: Canadian Food Inspection Agency

Breeding   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

Federally unregulated; follows provincial possession rules. Prohibited where keeping is banned (Alberta), legal where the species is allowed (SK/ON/QC/BC). Commercial breeders everywhere also face municipal business-licensing, zoning, and provincial animal-welfare standards.

Sources: Canadian Food Inspection Agency

Selling or giving away   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

Federally unregulated within Canada; follows provincial rules and municipal pet-shop / commercial-breeder licensing. Prohibited in Alberta (sale/distribution of a declared pest is banned); legal in SK/ON/QC/BC subject to local business rules.

Sources: Canadian Food Inspection Agency

Transport & import   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

Bringing a pet rat INTO Canada is permissive federally: the CFIA does not require an import permit or veterinary health certificate for pet rodents — you simply declare the animal to the Canada Border Services Agency. The big exceptions: any rodent originating from the continent of Africa is barred (plague/monkeypox rule), airlines may demand their own vet certificate, and exporting live rodents to the Eurasian Economic Union is currently suspended. Critically, your destination PROVINCE's rules still apply — you may not bring a rat into (or, arguably, through) Alberta at all.

Sources: Canadian Food Inspection Agency, CFIA, CFIA

Restrictions & responsibilities

Federal import is permit-free for pet rodents NOT from Africa — but a Rattus rattus originating from any African country is barred entry (and may be seized or destroyed). Airlines often require a veterinary health certificate even though the government does not, and exporting live rodents to the Eurasian Economic Union (Russia, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Armenia, Kyrgyzstan) is suspended until further notice.
  • Declare the animal as a pet to the CBSA at the border
  • Confirm it is not African-origin
  • Check your airline's own health-certificate rule

Forms: Bringing animals to Canada — CFIA · Where: Canada Border Services Agency / CFIA National Import Service Centre · Fees: No CFIA fee for pet rodents

Source: Canadian Food Inspection Agency, CFIA

The answer depends entirely on your province. Alberta bans all rats (do NOT bring one in); Saskatchewan, Ontario, Quebec, and British Columbia permit them. Always check your province (below) and your municipal bylaws (which can cap the number of animals or require a breeder licence).
  • Find your province below
  • Check your city/municipal animal bylaws

Source: Canadian Food Inspection Agency

The rule here isn't settled yet. Use our step-by-step guide to confirm with your agencies and send us what you find.

Help change this

How to help in Canada

Canada has no single national rule for keeping a pet roof rat (Rattus rattus); it is decided province by province, and the provinces diverge sharply. Saskatchewan explicitly lists the black rat as allowed captive wildlife; Ontario, Quebec, and British Columbia all permit it; and federally the CFIA allows import of a pet rat with no permit or health certificate, with one hard exception (no rodents originating from Africa). The outlier, and the one true prohibition in Canada, is Alberta. Under the Agricultural Pests Act and its Pest and Nuisance Control Regulation, the entire genus Rattus is a declared pest, and the Government of Alberta states that it is illegal to own pet rats in Alberta. There is no exemption for a tame, captive-bred animal kept indoors. The rule was written to keep wild Norway rats (Rattus norvegicus) from establishing breeding colonies on Alberta's farmland, but as written it also covers domesticated pet rats that pose none of that agricultural risk and have never founded a wild population.

The ask: Ask Alberta to add a narrow exemption to the Pest and Nuisance Control Regulation for tame, captive-bred companion rats kept indoors, the same kind of carve-out that lets neighbouring provinces allow them safely. The case rests on a cost-benefit judgment that is Alberta's to make. The province already permits cats and dogs, which are themselves non-native and documented to harm native wildlife, because their companionship is judged worth the trade-off. Whether the limited additional risk of a few sterile, tame, indoor-only pet rats, which have never founded a wild colony, is similarly outweighed by their value as companions is a question to put to the decision-makers, not a conclusion to assert. The change is to the regulation itself (a matter for the Minister of Agriculture and Irrigation and your MLA), not a favour the rat-control program can grant, because the program is correctly applying the law as written. Outside Alberta, no change is needed to keep a pet roof rat; confirm your province's rule and your municipal bylaws.

Where the lever really is: Branch (b): the law as written. The barrier is a deliberate statutory and regulatory listing, not a clerk's misreading. Alberta's Pest and Nuisance Control Regulation, made under the Agricultural Pests Act, declares the whole genus Rattus a pest, and the Government of Alberta's rat-control page states that it is illegal to own pet rats in Alberta, with no pet exemption. The rat-control program is applying that regulation as drafted, so emailing the program to ask permission, or appealing its decision, will not work. The fix is to amend the regulation to add a captive-bred companion-animal exemption, a decision for the Minister of Agriculture and Irrigation acting on public and political input. The correct lever is the legislature: your MLA and the Minister. For the other relevant provinces (SK, ON, QC, BC) there is no law-as-written problem to fix; the roof rat is already permitted, so they are a confirm-your-province check, not advocacy targets. On the species-not-domestication point, the fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus) is itself the wild brown rat, domesticated only in the 19th century, so a captive-bred Rattus rattus is the same case one species over: https://blonderoofrat.com/how-the-sewer-rat-became-the-fancy-rat/.

Where to send it (more than one channel helps):

  • Members of the Legislative Assembly of Alberta — official MLA directory / 'find your MLA' (legislature) — official contact page
    The prohibition lives in a regulation the Minister and Cabinet control, so the change must come through the political/legislative branch. This official Legislative Assembly page lets any Alberta resident look up and contact their own MLA — the representative who can raise a regulatory amendment or relay constituent demand to the Minister of Agriculture and Irrigation. Use it to write your own MLA; never address an individual member by name picked at random.
  • Elections Alberta — Member of the Legislative Assembly (MLA) search (legislature) — official contact page
    An independent official tool to confirm which MLA represents your address, in case you are unsure of your constituency before contacting them via the Assembly directory above.
  • Alberta Rat Control Program (Alberta Agriculture and Irrigation) — official program inbox (executive / agency) — rats@gov.ab.ca
    Secondary channel. This is the official inbox of the program that administers the declared-pest rule. It cannot grant a pet exemption on its own (the regulation must change first), but a polite written request for the government's current position on tame captive-bred companion rats, and for whether a narrow exemption could be recommended to the Minister, puts the ask on record with the administering body and can be cited when you write your MLA. Verified on the Government of Alberta rat-control program page.

A starting-point message — please put it in your own words; a short personal note carries far more weight than an identical form letter:

English
To my MLA / the Minister of Agriculture and Irrigation,

I am writing about Alberta's prohibition on keeping pet rats. Under the Pest and Nuisance Control Regulation, the entire genus Rattus is a declared pest, so even a tame, captive-bred companion rat is illegal to own here.

I understand and support the goal of keeping wild Norway rats from establishing in Alberta's farmland. But the regulation as written also bans domesticated pet rats that are captive-bred, hand-tame, kept entirely indoors, and never released, animals that pose none of the agricultural risk the rule was designed to stop and that have never founded a wild colony.

Saskatchewan, Ontario, Quebec, and British Columbia all allow these pets safely. The issue is not whether a rat can be domesticated; it plainly can. The dog descends from the wolf and the cat from a wild felid, yet both are recognised as domestic because of generations bred for tameness. The fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus) is itself the wild brown rat, domesticated only in the 19th century, so a captive-bred pet rat is the same case. The issue is simply that the species is on a list with no exemption for companion animals.

This is a cost-benefit judgment that belongs to Alberta. The province already permits cats and dogs, themselves non-native and documented to kill native wildlife, because their companionship is judged worth the trade-off. The narrow question is whether the limited additional risk of a few sterile, tame, indoor-only pet rats, which have never founded a wild colony, is outweighed by their value as companions. I am not asking you to reach a particular conclusion, only to weigh that question, which neighbouring provinces have already answered by allowing these pets while keeping their own wild-rat controls in place.

I respectfully ask you to support adding a narrow exemption to the Pest and Nuisance Control Regulation for tame, captive-bred rats kept indoors as pets, while leaving the wild-rat controls fully in place.

Thank you for considering this.

Sincerely,
[Your name]
[Your town and constituency]

Did you take action, or get a response? Tell us — it helps the next person, and we track what actually works.

Official sources

Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Germany

Summary. Germany is one of the cleanest 'yes' countries for keeping a roof rat. It uses a negative-list system (any animal may be kept unless a law bans it), and the black rat (Hausratte, Rattus rattus) is named-and-excluded by binomial from the federal species-protection annex. Although wild R. rattus is a Red List native mammal, Anlage 1 of the Bundesartenschutzverordnung (BArtSchV) lists both Rattus rattus and Rattus norvegicus as exceptions (mit Ausnahme von) to the 'specially protected' status that covers other native mammals, so a captive specimen has the exact same unregulated standing as the common fancy rat (R. norvegicus), with no registration, no origin certificate, and no CITES paperwork. Neither species is on the EU list of invasive alien species of Union concern (Reg. 1143/2014), so no EU keep/breed/sell/transport ban applies. No Bundesland dangerous-animal ordinance (Gefahrtierverordnung) covers small rodents, so keeping is uniform across all 16 states. The only live conditions sit at the welfare and commercial tiers: §2 TierSchG requires species-appropriate, behaviour-appropriate housing (R. rattus is strongly arboreal, so tall climbing enclosures), and crossing into a commercial operation triggers a §11 TierSchG Erlaubnis (the threshold for rodents is more than 300 young per year under the AVV TierSchG, or any business-like trading for profit). Hobby keeping, hobby breeding, and free or occasional private transfer need no permit. The one genuinely unclear point is importing a roof rat from a non-EU third country, because rodents fall outside the EU pet-travel rules and national veterinary-certificate requirements vary by port. Never release a roof rat into the wild.

Cross-checked against official government sources.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-14

Germany operates a negative-list system: any animal may be privately kept unless a specific law bans it, and no law bans R. rattus. The Bundesartenschutzverordnung (BArtSchV) Anlage 1 designates mammals (Mammalia spp. / Saeugetiere) as specially protected but lists an explicit exception block, and both 'Rattus norvegicus' (Wanderratte) and 'Rattus rattus' (Hausratte) appear by name in that 'mit Ausnahme von' exclusion, so the roof rat carries zero special protection despite wild populations being Red-Listed. Consequently no registration with the lower nature-conservation authority and no origin/CITES certificate is required. No EU bar applies either: neither Rattus species is on the EU list of invasive alien species of Union concern (Reg. 1143/2014). No Bundesland dangerous-animal ordinance (Gefahrtierverordnung) covers small rodents. The only keeping rule is §2 TierSchG: the keeper must provide species-appropriate and behaviour-appropriate feeding, care, and housing and have the necessary knowledge and skills; because R. rattus is arboreal, this implies tall climbing enclosures, enforced ex-post by the local Veterinaeramt only on complaint.

Sources: Bundesministerium der Justiz / gesetze-im-internet.de (federal statute portal), Bundesministerium der Justiz / gesetze-im-internet.de, Bundesministerium der Justiz / gesetze-im-internet.de, European Commission, DG Environment

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-14

Hobby breeding is unregulated: a private citizen may breed roof rats without a permit, registration, fee, or inspection. All breeders are still bound by §11b TierSchG (the Qualzucht / torture-breeding prohibition), but R. rattus is rarely bred for the extreme mutations (hairlessness, tailless, etc.) that trigger it. Breeding only becomes regulated when it is gewerbsmaessig (commercial): §11(1) sentence 1 No. 8(a) TierSchG requires a prior Erlaubnis from the local Veterinaeramt to commercially breed or keep vertebrates. The threshold is set in the AVV TierSchG (No. 12.2.1.5.1), which assumes commercial activity for rodents (Maeuse, Hamster, Ratten, Gerbils) at more than 300 young animals (Jungtiere) per year. A commercial breeder must pass a Sachkundenachweis (proof of competence), a Zuverlaessigkeitspruefung (reliability check), and an on-site facility inspection. This commercial layer applies identically to every vertebrate species, not just R. rattus.

Sources: Bundesministerium der Justiz / gesetze-im-internet.de, Bundesregierung / verwaltungsvorschriften-im-internet.de, Bundesministerium der Justiz / gesetze-im-internet.de

Selling or giving away   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-14

Private, occasional, non-business transfer (giving away a litter, an occasional small-scale sale) is unregulated: no health certificate, registration, bill of sale, or species-protection paperwork is required, because the BArtSchV exemption removes any CITES/origin-document duty for R. rattus. Regulation attaches only to commercial dealing: §11(1) sentence 1 No. 8(b) TierSchG requires an Erlaubnis from the local Veterinaeramt for anyone who commercially trades in vertebrates (gewerbsmaessiger Handel mit Wirbeltieren), defined by the AVV TierSchG by business-like intent (planmaessig, fortgesetzt und mit der Absicht der Gewinnerzielung) rather than a fixed volume. A commercial seller must also give the buyer written care information about the species. Because the predominant case for a hobbyist keeper is free or occasional private transfer, the headline status is legal, with the §11 permit applying only to a business-like dealer.

Sources: Bundesministerium der Justiz / gesetze-im-internet.de, Bundesregierung / verwaltungsvorschriften-im-internet.de, Bundesministerium der Justiz / gesetze-im-internet.de (federal statute portal)

Transport & import   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-14

Domestic transport within Germany (including between Bundeslaender) is entirely unregulated: there are no internal border checks for pets and no movement documents, the only condition being general §2 TierSchG welfare during transit (appropriate carrier with adequate space, ventilation, and protection from temperature extremes). Moving a roof rat into Germany from another EU country is also simple: rodents are explicitly outside the EU pet-travel rules (Reg. 576/2013, which target rabies in dogs, cats, and ferrets), so no EU pet passport or microchip is required, and R. rattus is not on the EU invasive-species Union list (Reg. 1143/2014), so no IAS transport ban applies. The single open point is import from a non-EU third country, handled at activity level here but flagged as unclear in notes and routed to Zoll/BMEL. Never release a roof rat into the wild (intentional release of a captive animal is an offence under animal-welfare and ecological law).

Sources: Bundesministerium der Justiz / gesetze-im-internet.de, Generalzolldirektion (German Customs), European Commission, DG Environment

Restrictions & responsibilities

Commercial (gewerbsmaessig) breeding or trading of vertebrates requires a prior Erlaubnis under §11(1) TierSchG from the local Veterinaeramt. For rodents, breeding is assumed commercial above more than 300 young animals per year (AVV TierSchG No. 12.2.1.5.1); trading is assumed commercial by business-like, profit-seeking intent. Hobby breeding and free/occasional private transfer are exempt.
  • Determine whether your activity is gewerbsmaessig: for breeding, more than 300 young/year (AVV TierSchG); for selling, regular business-like trading for profit.
  • If commercial, apply for the §11 TierSchG Erlaubnis at your local Veterinaeramt BEFORE starting operations.
  • Pass the Sachkundenachweis (proof of competence) via a vocational qualification or a Fachgespraech with the official state veterinarian (Amtstierarzt).
  • Pass the Zuverlaessigkeitspruefung (reliability check) and an on-site facility inspection (lighting, ventilation, hygiene, enclosure sizes; check local Baurecht/zoning).
  • Commercial sellers must additionally give each buyer written species-care information at the point of sale.

Where: Local Veterinaeramt (oertliches Veterinaeramt / Amtstierarzt) · Fees: No fixed national fee; permit processing scales with administrative effort and economic advantage, roughly 50 to 10,000 EUR plus travel costs of inspecting officials.

Source: Bundesministerium der Justiz / gesetze-im-internet.de, Bundesregierung / verwaltungsvorschriften-im-internet.de

§2 TierSchG requires species-appropriate, behaviour-appropriate housing. Because R. rattus is strongly arboreal (longer balancing tail, larger ears, naturally lives in high places), a wide-but-short enclosure that might satisfy a terrestrial rodent can fall short, and the local Veterinaeramt may issue corrective orders. This is an ongoing welfare duty enforced ex-post (on complaint or observed cruelty), not a pre-acquisition permit or registration.
  • Provide a tall enclosure with vertical climbing space, multiple levels, secure bar spacing (commonly cited maxima around 1.5 cm, 1.0 cm for juveniles), ventilation, and social housing.
  • Use the BMEL Saeugetiergutachten and TVT Merkblatt 160 as the practical interpretive standard for §2 TierSchG.
  • Keep at least two rats together (rats are social); never single-house.

Where: Local Veterinaeramt (enforces §2 TierSchG; no filing required by a private keeper)

Source: Bundesministerium der Justiz / gesetze-im-internet.de

Importing a roof rat from a NON-EU third country is the one unclear area. Rodents are outside the EU pet-travel rules (Reg. 576/2013, which cover dogs/cats/ferrets and rabies), so no EU pet passport applies, but the German border inspection post (Veterinaergrenzkontrollstelle) may require a national veterinary health certificate (Tiergesundheitsbescheinigung) depending on the origin country's epidemiological status and the port of entry. Domestic and intra-EU movement need no such document. Confirm the exact certificate with Zoll/BMEL before any third-country import.
  • Domestic / intra-EU: no passport, microchip, or permit for rodents; transport with §2 TierSchG welfare conditions only.
  • Non-EU import: contact German Customs (Zoll) and/or BMEL in advance for the required Tiergesundheitsbescheinigung and any zoonosis-testing requirements for the genus Rattus at your intended border inspection post.
  • Never release a roof rat into the wild.

Where: German Customs (Zoll) central information desk / BMEL; the Veterinaergrenzkontrollstelle at the port of entry.

Source: Generalzolldirektion (German Customs)

Never release a roof rat into the wild. Intentional release of a captive-bred animal is an offence under animal-welfare and ecological law, and R. rattus is an invasive species globally. Rehome responsibly through free adoption with vetting.

Source: Bundesministerium der Justiz / gesetze-im-internet.de

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Official sources

  • Anlage 1 BArtSchV (Bundesartenschutzverordnung): Mammalia spp. specially protected, with explicit exception block naming 'Rattus norvegicus' and 'Rattus rattus' (mit Ausnahme von), removing both from 'besonders geschuetzt' status — Bundesministerium der Justiz / gesetze-im-internet.de (federal statute portal)
  • § 11 TierSchG (Tierschutzgesetz): Erlaubnispflicht; §11(1) S.1 Nr. 8 requires a permit to gewerbsmaessig (a) breed/keep vertebrates (except farm animals and enclosed game) or (b) trade in vertebrates — Bundesministerium der Justiz / gesetze-im-internet.de
  • § 2 TierSchG: anyone keeping an animal must feed, care for, and house it appropriately to its species and needs (verhaltensgerechte Unterbringung) and possess the necessary knowledge and skills — Bundesministerium der Justiz / gesetze-im-internet.de
  • Allgemeine Verwaltungsvorschrift zur Durchfuehrung des Tierschutzgesetzes (AVV TierSchG), No. 12.2.1.5.1: rodents (Maeuse, Hamster, Ratten, Gerbils) assumed gewerbsmaessig at more than 300 Jungtiere per year — Bundesregierung / verwaltungsvorschriften-im-internet.de
  • § 39 BNatSchG (Bundesnaturschutzgesetz): general protection of wild-living animals and plants (the baseline that BArtSchV Anlage 1 modifies; R. rattus excepted) — Bundesministerium der Justiz / gesetze-im-internet.de
  • EU list of invasive alien species of Union concern (Regulation (EU) 1143/2014; consolidated Union list, 114 species as of the Aug 2025 update). NEITHER Rattus rattus NOR Rattus norvegicus is listed; listed rodents are squirrels/chipmunks, listed mammals include Myocastor coypus, Ondatra zibethicus, Procyon lotor — European Commission, DG Environment
  • Zoll (German Customs): rules for bringing pets (Heimtiere) from non-EU states; EU pet-travel rules (Reg. 576/2013) cover only dogs/cats/ferrets, so rodents fall under national veterinary rules confirmed via Zoll/BMEL/the border veterinary post — Generalzolldirektion (German Customs)

Search terms: Rattus rattus, Hausratte, Dachratte, Schiffsratte, black rat, roof rat, ship rat, Wanderratte (= Rattus norvegicus, the Norway/fancy rat, for contrast), Tierschutzgesetz (TierSchG), Bundesartenschutzverordnung (BArtSchV).
