Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Spain

Summary. Earlier research wrongly treated the roof rat as banned nationwide; the environment ministry has now corrected that. On the Spanish mainland (and everywhere outside the Canary Islands) Rattus rattus is NOT a cataloged invasive species, so the Real Decreto 630/2013 Art. 7.1 possession/breeding/transport/trade ban does not apply there — keeping is instead governed by the 2023 animal-welfare law (Ley 7/2023) and its forthcoming companion-animal 'listado positivo' (positive list), which is still pending and not yet in force. In the Canary Islands, by contrast, R. rattus IS listed in the Catálogo Español de Especies Exóticas Invasoras for that territory alone, so there the Art. 7.1 ban (possess/breed/sell/transport live specimens) does apply. Commercial breeding or sale anywhere in Spain requires a núcleo zoológico (establishment) authorization from the relevant Comunidad Autónoma, and animal health/identification/movement of bred or traded animals falls under the Ministry of Agriculture. So the country-level reality is split: not prohibited on the mainland (welfare-regulated, positive list pending) but cataloged-and-prohibited in the Canaries.

Key points here are confirmed in writing by the responsible agency (see below).
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
Confirmed by the agencies.
  • Spain's environment ministry for ecological transition (biodiversity mailbox), written reply June 2026, corrected the prior nationwide-ban reading: Rattus rattus is included in the Catálogo Español de Especies Exóticas Invasoras EXCLUSIVELY for the case of the Canary Islands, not nationwide. The ministry also set out the competence split: invasive-species catalogues and exotic/wildlife matters sit with the environment ministry (natural heritage and biodiversity); the animal-welfare framework for companion animals is Ley 7/2023, with competence mainly at the social-rights/consumer ministry (which is also building the companion-animal positive list); animal health, identification, movement, and the sanitary conditions of breeding, trade and transport sit with the Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food; and authorization of núcleos zoológicos, breeding centres and establishment registries sits with the Comunidades Autónomas (regional governments). The practical effect: on the mainland R. rattus is not cataloged, so the Art. 7.1 ban does not reach it and keeping is permissible under the general welfare law pending the positive list; in the Canary Islands it is cataloged and the Art. 7.1 ban applies.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-11

On the Spanish mainland (and outside the Canary Islands), R. rattus is NOT in the Catálogo Español de EEI, so the RD 630/2013 Art. 7.1 possession ban does not apply and keeping is not prohibited; it is instead governed by the general animal-welfare framework of Ley 7/2023, with the companion-animal positive list still pending and not yet in force. In the Canary Islands, by contrast, R. rattus IS cataloged, so there Art. 7.1 prohibits possession of live specimens. The country-level reality is therefore 'legal on the mainland, prohibited in the Canaries'; confidence is medium because the forthcoming positive list could change mainland keepability once it takes effect.

Sources: BOE / Gobierno de España, MITECO, BOE / Gobierno de España

Breeding   Legal with a permit

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-11

On the mainland R. rattus is not cataloged, so the RD 630/2013 Art. 7.1 breeding ban does not apply there; breeding for sale or as an establishment requires a núcleo zoológico authorization from the relevant Comunidad Autónoma (the regional government that authorizes breeding centres and establishment registries), and animal health/identification of bred animals falls under the Ministry of Agriculture. In the Canary Islands, where R. rattus IS cataloged, Art. 7.1 prohibits reproduction of live specimens, so breeding there is barred. Country-level best fit is legal_with_permit (regional núcleo-zoológico authorization on the mainland); confidence medium pending the positive-list outcome.

Sources: BOE / Gobierno de España, BOE / Gobierno de España

Selling or giving away   Legal with a permit

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-11

On the mainland R. rattus is not cataloged, so the RD 630/2013 Art. 7.1 trade/commerce ban does not apply there; selling or commercially supplying live animals requires a núcleo zoológico authorization from the Comunidad Autónoma, with animal-health/identification/movement conditions under the Ministry of Agriculture, and welfare/transfer requirements under Ley 7/2023. In the Canary Islands, where the species IS cataloged, Art. 7.1 prohibits 'tráfico y comercio de ejemplares vivos,' so sale/transfer there is barred. Private free rehoming on the mainland is not banned but is subject to the Ley 7/2023 welfare framework; commercial sale needs the establishment authorization — hence legal_with_permit at country level.

Sources: BOE / Gobierno de España, BOE / Gobierno de España

Transport & import   Legal with a permit

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-11

On the mainland R. rattus is not cataloged, so the RD 630/2013 Art. 7.1 transport ban does not apply there; movement of bred or traded animals is instead subject to the animal-health, identification and sanitary-movement rules administered by the Ministry of Agriculture (and ordinary welfare-in-transport requirements). In the Canary Islands, where the species IS cataloged, Art. 7.1 prohibits 'transporte' of live specimens. R. rattus is not on the EU Union list, so there is no EU-level border ban; non-commercial pet movement within the EU follows Reg. (EU) 576/2013, but the Canary-Islands catalogue prohibition takes effect on Canarian soil. Country-level best fit is legal_with_permit (sanitary/movement conditions on the mainland); never release.

Sources: BOE / Gobierno de España, EU / EUR-Lex

Restrictions & responsibilities

Territorial split. CANARY ISLANDS: R. rattus is a cataloged invasive species (RD 630/2013 Art. 7.1), so possessing, breeding, selling/giving or transporting a live one is prohibited there. MAINLAND (and elsewhere outside the Canaries): R. rattus is NOT cataloged, so it is not banned — keeping is governed by Ley 7/2023 (welfare; companion-animal positive list still pending/not in force), commercial breeding or sale needs a Comunidad-Autónoma núcleo zoológico authorization, and animal health/identification/movement fall under the Ministry of Agriculture. Never release anywhere.
  • Mainland: keep under the Ley 7/2023 welfare framework; watch for the forthcoming companion-animal positive list
  • Mainland commercial breeding/sale: obtain a núcleo zoológico authorization from the relevant Comunidad Autónoma; meet Ministry of Agriculture animal-health/movement rules
  • Canary Islands: do not acquire, breed, sell or move R. rattus (cataloged invasive, Art. 7.1 ban)
  • If advocating: ask the positive-list rulemaking ministry to include captive-bred R. rattus; for the Canaries, the formal exclusión/de-cataloguing procedure

Where: Comunidad Autónoma (núcleo zoológico authorization); environment ministry — biodiversity (Catálogo de EEI / Canaries de-cataloguing); social-rights/consumer ministry (positive list)

Source: BOE / Gobierno de España, BOE / Gobierno de España

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Help change this

How to help in Spain

Spain's treatment of the roof rat (Rattus rattus) is territorial, not a blanket ban. The environment ministry confirmed this in writing in June 2026. The species is in the Catálogo Español de Especies Exóticas Invasoras (Real Decreto 630/2013) only for the Canary Islands. On the mainland and elsewhere it is not a cataloged invasive species, so the Article 7.1 possession/breeding/transport/trade ban does not reach it there. Mainland keeping is governed by the 2023 animal-welfare law (Ley 7/2023), under which the companion-animal 'listado positivo' (positive list) of species that may be kept as pets is still being written and is not yet in force. The concern is what happens when that list takes effect. The law generally excludes catalogue-listed invasive species from the positive list. Because R. rattus is cataloged in one territory (the Canaries), it is an edge case: a captive-bred domestic line that is legal to keep on the mainland today could be left off the national positive list by default unless the rulemaking treats it deliberately. The barrier is not a current prohibition. It is the risk that a future list closes the door that is open today. The already-permitted 'fancy rat' (Rattus norvegicus) is itself the wild brown rat, domesticated only in the 19th century, so a captive-bred Rattus rattus is the same case one species over.

The ask: Ask the ministry responsible for the Ley 7/2023 companion-animal positive list (social-rights/consumer) to include captive-bred Rattus rattus on the listado positivo, or, failing inclusion, to handle it through registration and welfare conditions, so that a species which is lawful to keep on the mainland today remains keepable once the list takes effect. Ask the rulemaking to address the partially-cataloged edge case explicitly: because R. rattus is cataloged only for the Canary Islands and is not an invasive species on the mainland, its captive-bred, indoor, never-released lineages should not be removed from the national positive list by the general 'no catálogo species' exclusion, which was designed for species cataloged across Spain. The already-permitted fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus) is itself the wild brown rat, domesticated only in the 19th century, so a captive-bred Rattus rattus is the same case one species over (see https://blonderoofrat.com/how-the-sewer-rat-became-the-fancy-rat/ ). On the invasive-species concern that underlies the exclusion, the question is a cost-benefit one for Spain to decide. Cats and dogs are also non-native across most of Spain and are documented to harm native and especially island wildlife, yet are permitted everywhere as pets. Whether the limited additional risk of a few sterilized or altered, tame, indoor-only domesticated rats is similarly outweighed by their value as companions is a judgment for the ministry to make. Separately, for keepers in the Canary Islands, ask the environment ministry about the formal exclusión (de-cataloguing) procedure under Article 64 of Ley 42/2007 and RD 630/2013 to remove captive-origin R. rattus from the catalogue for that territory.

Where the lever really is: Two distinct levers, selected by territory and by question. (1) POSITIVE LIST is a rulemaking lever at the social-rights/consumer ministry (Dirección General de Derechos de los Animales), which owns the Ley 7/2023 'listado positivo' royal decree still in progress. The ask is inclusion of captive-bred R. rattus, with explicit treatment of the partial-catalogue edge case (cataloged only in the Canaries, not on the mainland). This is the primary lever because mainland keeping is otherwise already lawful and the only future risk is exclusion-by-default from the positive list. (2) CANARY-ISLANDS DE-CATALOGUING is an agency-procedure lever at the environment ministry (which owns the Catálogo de EEI). The formal exclusión procedure (Art. 64 Ley 42/2007 + RD 630/2013) is open to any citizen or organisation with scientific justification and is the route to lift the Art. 7.1 ban for the Canaries. It is secondary because it only matters for keepers in that territory. Authorization of breeding/sale establishments (núcleos zoológicos) is a separate Comunidad-Autónoma matter, and animal health/movement sits with the Ministry of Agriculture. Neither is an advocacy barrier, only the ordinary permitting layer. No front-desk clarification changes any of this, and the prior positive-list public-comment window is closed, so route the positive-list ask through the rulemaking ministry's mailbox and consider a keeper-rights ally to carry the scientific case.

Where to send it (more than one channel helps):

  • Ministerio de Derechos Sociales, Consumo y Agenda 2030 — Dirección General de Derechos de los Animales (Ley 7/2023 listado positivo rulemaking) (executive / agency) — official contact page
    This is the ministry writing the Ley 7/2023 companion-animal positive list — the instrument that will decide, going forward, whether captive-bred R. rattus may be kept as a pet on the mainland once the list is in force. It is the correct office to ask that captive-bred R. rattus be INCLUDED on the positive list and that the partial-catalogue edge case (cataloged only in the Canaries) be resolved deliberately rather than by the default 'no catálogo species' exclusion. The prior public-comment window (17 Apr – 8 May 2026) is closed, so engage via the ministry's published rulemaking channel rather than as an open consultation.
  • Environment ministry — biodiversity sub-directorate (Catálogo Español de EEI): exclusión / de-cataloguing procedure for the Canary Islands listing (executive / agency) — buzon-sgb@miteco.es
    This office owns the invasive-species catalogue and confirmed in June 2026 that R. rattus is cataloged ONLY for the Canary Islands. Its formal 'Catalogación o descatalogación de taxones' procedure (Art. 64 Ley 42/2007 + RD 630/2013) is open to any citizen or organisation to request exclusión (de-listing) with scientific justification. This is the correct lever ONLY for the Canaries, where the Art. 7.1 ban actually applies — it is irrelevant on the mainland, where the species is not cataloged.
  • Federación FAUNA — keeper/breeder rights federation (advocacy ally, not a government body) (executive / agency) — official contact page
    Spain's principal keeper/breeder federation, active in the listado-positivo rulemaking. As an organisation it can carry the scientific/husbandry case for INCLUDING captive-bred R. rattus on the positive list (and, for Canaries keepers, a de-cataloguing petition) more effectively than a lone keeper. Engage as an ally to the rulemaking ask, not as a substitute for it. (Do NOT route this to the conservation-aligned Coalición para el Listado Positivo.)

A starting-point message — please put it in your own words; a short personal note carries far more weight than an identical form letter:

English
To: Dirección General de Derechos de los Animales (Ministerio de Derechos Sociales, Consumo y Agenda 2030)
Re: Treatment of captive-bred Rattus rattus in the Ley 7/2023 companion-animal positive list (listado positivo)

Dear Sir or Madam,

I am writing regarding the welfare and legal status of domesticated roof rats (Rattus rattus). The environment ministry has confirmed that R. rattus is in the Catálogo Español de Especies Exóticas Invasoras only for the case of the Canary Islands, and is not a cataloged invasive species on the mainland, where keeping it is governed by Ley 7/2023 rather than by any catalogue ban.

My concern is the forthcoming companion-animal positive list. Because the law generally excludes catalogue-listed species from the positive list, a species cataloged in only one territory (the Canary Islands) risks being left off the national list by default, even though on the mainland it is not an invasive species and is lawful to keep today.

I ask: (1) that captive-bred Rattus rattus be included on the listado positivo, so that a domesticated, indoor, never-released line that is keepable on the mainland today remains keepable once the list is in force; and (2) that the rulemaking address the partial-catalogue situation explicitly, distinguishing the Canary-Islands listing from mainland status, rather than applying the general 'no catálogo species' exclusion to a species that is invasive in only one region. If full inclusion is not possible, please advise whether captive-bred lineages could instead be handled through registration and welfare conditions.

The already-permitted fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus) is itself the wild brown rat, domesticated only in the 19th century. A captive-bred Rattus rattus is the same case one species over.

On the invasive-species concern that underlies the exclusion, this is a cost-benefit question for Spain to decide. Cats and dogs are also non-native across most of Spain and are documented to harm native and especially island wildlife, yet are permitted everywhere as pets. Whether the limited additional risk of a few sterilized or altered, tame, indoor-only domesticated rats is similarly outweighed by their value as companions is a judgment for the ministry to make.

Thank you for your time and for your work on animal welfare.

Sincerely,
[Your name]
[Your town / province]
[Date]
Español
A: Dirección General de Derechos de los Animales (Ministerio de Derechos Sociales, Consumo y Agenda 2030)
Asunto: Tratamiento de la Rattus rattus criada en cautividad en el listado positivo de animales de compañía de la Ley 7/2023

Estimados señores:

Les escribo en relación con el bienestar y el estatus jurídico de las ratas domésticas (Rattus rattus). El ministerio competente en medio ambiente ha confirmado que la R. rattus está incluida en el Catálogo Español de Especies Exóticas Invasoras únicamente para el caso de las Islas Canarias, y no es especie catalogada invasora en la península, donde su tenencia se rige por la Ley 7/2023 y no por ninguna prohibición del Catálogo.

Mi preocupación es el futuro listado positivo de animales de compañía. Dado que la ley excluye con carácter general del listado positivo a las especies catalogadas, una especie catalogada en un solo territorio (las Islas Canarias) corre el riesgo de quedar fuera del listado nacional por defecto, pese a que en la península no es una especie invasora y hoy su tenencia es lícita.

Les ruego: (1) que la Rattus rattus criada en cautividad se incluya en el listado positivo, de modo que un linaje doméstico, mantenido en el interior del hogar y nunca liberado, que hoy puede tenerse en la península, siga pudiendo mantenerse cuando el listado entre en vigor; y (2) que el desarrollo reglamentario aborde de forma expresa la situación de catalogación parcial, distinguiendo la inclusión en Canarias del estatus peninsular, en lugar de aplicar la exclusión general de 'especies catalogadas' a una especie que es invasora en una sola región. Si la inclusión plena no fuera posible, les ruego me indiquen si los linajes criados en cautividad podrían regularse mediante registro y condiciones de bienestar.

La ya permitida rata doméstica (Rattus norvegicus) es la propia rata parda salvaje, domesticada solo en el siglo XIX. Una Rattus rattus criada en cautividad es el mismo caso una especie más allá.

Respecto a la preocupación por el carácter invasor que motiva la exclusión, se trata de una cuestión de coste-beneficio que corresponde decidir a España. Los gatos y los perros son también especies no autóctonas en casi toda España y está documentado que perjudican a la fauna autóctona, en especial a la insular, y aun así se permiten en todas partes como animales de compañía. Si el limitado riesgo adicional de unas pocas ratas domésticas esterilizadas o alteradas, dóciles y mantenidas siempre en interior queda igualmente compensado por su valor como animales de compañía es un juicio que corresponde hacer al ministerio.

Les agradezco su tiempo y la labor que realizan en favor del bienestar animal.

Atentamente,
[Su nombre]
[Su localidad / provincia]
[Fecha]

Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › France

Summary. In metropolitan France a captive-bred roof rat is legal to keep, hobby-breed, and give away, and the species-vs-domestication line does not, in practice, add a permit. The roof rat is non-domestic (the Arrêté du 11 août 2006 lists only 'les races domestiques du rat (Rattus norvegicus)' among the rodents), so it is governed by the Code de l'environnement and the Arrêté du 8 octobre 2018. But Annexe 2 of that order places Rattus rattus in the catch-all 'Toutes les autres espèces de Rodentia' row, which is column (a) 'Pas de formalité' (no formality) for 1 to 40 adult animals; only 41 or more triggers a certificat de capacité. Marking and I-FAP registration apply only to protected or CITES species (Article 3 of the same order), so they do not apply to the roof rat. A sale (vente) must come with a written document d'information (Art. L413-8); a free transfer between private persons does not. R. rattus is not on the EU Union list (Reg. 1143/2014) or France's metropolitan invasive Arrêté du 14 février 2018, so there is no keeping or sale ban. Commercial breeding or selling to the public is a separate, permitted-only regime (établissement authorization plus, for trade, Code rural Art. L214-6). Two limits: the species is managed as invasive in the French overseas territories (DROM-COM), where local decrees prohibit it; and the 2021 welfare law created a future 'positive list' (Art. L413-1A) whose implementing arrêté is still unpublished, a watch item rather than a current restriction.

Cross-checked against official government sources.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-13

The roof rat is non-domestic (the Arrêté du 11 août 2006 lists only 'les races domestiques du rat (Rattus norvegicus)' among the Muridae), so it is governed by the Code de l'environnement (Art. L413-1 et seq.) and the Arrêté du 8 octobre 2018. Annexe 2 of that order places R. rattus in the catch-all row 'Toutes les autres espèces de Rodentia, hors espèces figurant en annexe A du règlement (CE) n° 338/97 susvisé et hors espèces protégées en application de l'article L. 411-1 du code de l'environnement', for which column (a) 'Pas de formalité' covers 'De 1 à 40' adults and only '41 et plus' triggers a certificat de capacité. So keeping 1 to 40 adult roof rats requires no declaration and no permit. Marking and I-FAP registration apply only to protected or CITES species (Article 3 of the order), not to R. rattus. The species is not on the EU Union list or the metropolitan invasive list, so there is no keeping ban. Overseas territories (DROM-COM) manage it as invasive and may prohibit it locally.

Sources: Ministère de l'Écologie, Ministère de la Transition écologique, Ministère de la Transition écologique

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-13

Non-commercial hobby breeding (élevage d'agrément) follows the same Annexe 2 thresholds as keeping: below 41 adult animals R. rattus sits in column (a) 'Pas de formalité', so no declaration and no breeding permit are required; offspring count toward the threshold only once adult. Reaching 41 or more adults moves the keeper into column (c), requiring a certificat de capacité (Art. L413-2) and an autorisation d'ouverture d'établissement (Art. L413-3). Breeding for profit or systematically producing litters for the public is a separate matter: it requires opening a declared establishment (autorisation préalable under Art. R413-8) and, as a pet-trade activity, falls under Code rural Art. L214-6. The L413-1A 'élevage de conservation' carve-out awaits its implementing decree.

Sources: Ministère de la Transition écologique, Légifrance, Légifrance

Selling or giving away   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-13

A private person may give away or sell a small number of captive-bred roof rats without a permit. The attestation de cession and identification-document formalities of Art. R413-23-4 apply only 'pour les animaux des espèces mentionnées à l'article L. 413-6' (marked, i.e. protected or CITES species), which R. rattus is not, so they do not bind a roof-rat transfer. A sale (vente) of a live non-domestic animal must be accompanied by a written document d'information on the animal's characteristics, needs, and upkeep (Art. L413-8); a gratuitous transfer between private persons does not require it. Selling commercially or systematically to the public requires operating a declared pet-trade establishment (autorisation préalable, Art. R413-8; Code rural Art. L214-6). R. rattus is not on the EU Union list, so there is no sale ban.

Sources: Légifrance, Légifrance, Légifrance, EU / EUR-Lex

Transport & import   Legal

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-13

Moving a captive-bred roof rat within metropolitan France is legal for private individuals, subject to humane, escape-proof transport. There is no EU pet-passport or harmonised health-certificate scheme for rodents (Reg. (EU) 576/2013 does not cover them), so intra-EU non-commercial movement follows the destination country's national rules. Importing from outside the EU triggers veterinary controls: the Arrêté du 19 juillet 2002 (Annexe 18 model certificate for rodents) requires a health certificate from an official veterinarian of the exporting country and presentation at an approved Border Control Post. R. rattus is not on the EU Union list or the metropolitan invasive Arrêté du 14 février 2018, so there is no import ban for métropole. The French OVERSEAS territories (Réunion, Mayotte, Martinique, Guadeloupe and others) manage R. rattus as a damaging invasive species and local decrees prohibit its introduction, detention, transport, and sale, so transport into or within those territories is unlawful.

Sources: Ministère de l'Agriculture, EU / EUR-Lex, EU / EUR-Lex, Ministère de la Transition écologique

Restrictions & responsibilities

Below 41 adult animals there is no formality: the roof rat falls in column (a) 'Pas de formalité' of Annexe 2 of the Arrêté du 8 octobre 2018. Reaching 41 or more adults moves the keeper into column (c), which requires a certificat de capacité and an autorisation d'ouverture d'établissement. The certificat de capacité is a professional-grade credential (theory dossier, logged practical experience, defence before a departmental commission, facility inspection), so the practical ceiling for a hobbyist is 40 adults.
  • Stay at or below 40 adult animals to remain in the 'Pas de formalité' tier
  • To exceed 40 adults, obtain a certificat de capacité and an autorisation d'ouverture d'établissement

Where: Préfecture de département (DDETSPP / DREAL) for the certificat de capacité and establishment authorization

Source: Ministère de la Transition écologique

A sale (vente) of a live roof rat must be accompanied by a written document d'information on the animal's characteristics, needs, and upkeep (Art. L413-8). A free transfer between private persons does not require it. Selling commercially or systematically to the public requires operating a declared pet-trade establishment (autorisation préalable, Art. R413-8; Code rural Art. L214-6). The attestation de cession / I-FAP formalities of Art. R413-23-4 do not apply, because they are limited to marked (protected/CITES) species.
  • On a sale, give the buyer a written document d'information (Art. L413-8)
  • Do not sell commercially or systematically without a declared establishment

Source: Légifrance, Légifrance

Importing from outside the EU requires a veterinary health certificate (Arrêté du 19 juillet 2002, Annexe 18 model for rodents) issued by an official veterinarian of the exporting country, with presentation at an approved Border Control Post. There is no EU pet passport for rodents; intra-EU non-commercial movement follows the destination state's rules. Never release a roof rat into the wild.
  • For non-EU import, obtain the Annexe 18 veterinary health certificate and clear an approved Border Control Post
  • For intra-EU movement, check the destination country's national rules for rodents

Where: Border Control Post (Poste de contrôle frontalier)

Source: Ministère de l'Agriculture

In the French overseas territories (DROM-COM: Réunion, Mayotte, Martinique, Guadeloupe and others) R. rattus is managed as a damaging invasive species and local prefectural/ministerial decrees prohibit its introduction, detention, transport, reproduction, and sale. The metropolitan 'no formality' position does NOT apply there.

Where: Préfecture / DEAL of the territory concerned

Source: Ministère de la Transition écologique

  • Arrêté du 8 octobre 2018, Annexe 2: 'Toutes les autres espèces de Rodentia' in column (a) 'Pas de formalité' De 1 à 40, 41 et plus = certificat de capacité (R. norvegicus = déclaration from 1) — Ministère de la Transition écologique
  • Arrêté du 8 octobre 2018, Article 3: mandatory marking + national-file registration limited to L411-1/L411-2 protected and CITES (Reg. 338/97 Annexes A-D) species; R. rattus exempt — Ministère de la Transition écologique
  • Code de l'environnement Art. R413-23-4: attestation de cession / identification document obligations limited to 'animaux des espèces mentionnées à l'article L. 413-6' (marked species) — Légifrance
  • Code de l'environnement Art. L413-8: 'Toute vente d'un animal vivant d'une espèce non domestique' must include a document d'information (applies to sales, not gratuitous gifts) — Légifrance
  • Code de l'environnement Art. L413-1 A: positive list for non-domestic companion animals fixed by arrêté du ministre chargé de l'environnement; 'toute personne physique ou morale' may request inclusion, reasoned reply within six months (arrêté still pending) — Légifrance
  • Code rural Art. L214-6: pet-trade establishment declaration (élevage / vente) — Légifrance

  • Regulation (EU) 576/2013 on the non-commercial movement of pet animals: rodents not covered by the EU pet-passport scheme — EU / EUR-Lex

Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United Kingdom

Summary. In Great Britain, keeping and hobby-breeding a captive-bred roof rat is legal — it's omitted from the Dangerous Wild Animals Act 1976 and from the Invasive Alien Species (Enforcement and Permitting) Order 2019 possession bans. BUT the roof rat is on Schedule 9 of the Wildlife & Countryside Act 1981, so it's a strict-liability criminal offence to release it or let it escape into the wild (use escape-proof caging; you may not release a trapped one). Commercial breeding/selling needs a local-authority Animal Welfare licence (and inspectors may treat it as a non-domestic species). Sale is OUTRIGHT PROHIBITED in Northern Ireland (Wildlife (NI) Order 1985, Art. 15A). Importing one is excluded from the Pet Travel Scheme and needs an APHA rabies import licence (Form RM01) + up to 4 months quarantine.

Cross-checked against official government sources.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-07

No statute bans mere possession of a captive-bred roof rat: the genus Rattus (family Muridae) is absent from the Dangerous Wild Animals Act 1976 schedule, it's not under the Destructive Imported Animals Act 1932, and it's not on Schedule 2 of the Invasive Alien Species (Enforcement and Permitting) Order 2019 (the possession-ban list). Owners owe the Animal Welfare Act 2006 duty of care. Because R. rattus IS on Schedule 9 of the WCA 1981, releasing it or letting it escape is a criminal offence — and a trapped one may not be released back to the wild.

Sources: UK Government / legislation.gov.uk, UK Government / Defra, UK Government / legislation.gov.uk

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-07

Purely private, non-commercial hobby breeding is unregulated (no statutory litter limits), subject to the Animal Welfare Act 2006. The moment it becomes commercial (profit intent, >£1,000/yr gross from animal sales, dealing, or systematic advertising of litters), it requires a local-authority Animal Welfare licence under the Animal Welfare (Licensing of Activities Involving Animals) Regulations 2018 (England) / 2021 (Wales & Scotland). Never let breeding stock escape (Sch. 9).

Sources: Defra / local authorities, UK Government / legislation.gov.uk

Selling or giving away   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-07

GREAT BRITAIN: selling as a business needs a local-authority Animal Welfare licence (the 'business test' / £1,000 HMRC trading allowance); inspectors may classify the roof rat under 'Part I — other non-domestic mammals' (higher burden, invasive-species containment) rather than 'Part H — domestic small rodents'. Giving one away free is generally outside the commercial 'sale' test. NORTHERN IRELAND: selling, offering for sale, or transporting for sale is an OUTRIGHT CRIMINAL OFFENCE (Wildlife (NI) Order 1985, Art. 15A; R. rattus is on Sch. 9 Part 1) — no licensing pathway exists; even advertising is barred.

Sources: Defra / local authorities, DAERA / legislation.gov.uk

Transport & import   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-07

DOMESTIC: legal under the Welfare of Animals (Transport) Order 2006 — but use gnaw-proof, escape-proof carriers, because an escape in transit is a strict-liability offence (WCA 1981 s.14/Sch. 9). IMPORT: the roof rat is a rabies-susceptible non-native mammal EXCLUDED from the Pet Travel Scheme; you must apply for an APHA Rabies Import Licence (Form RM01) — non-EU origin means up to 4 months quarantine; EU origin may be exempt if captive-bred/kept since birth. Northern Ireland adds Windsor-Framework pre-notification. No CITES permit (not endangered).

Sources: APHA / UK Government, UK Government / legislation.gov.uk

Restrictions & responsibilities

The roof rat is on Schedule 9 of the Wildlife & Countryside Act 1981: it is a criminal offence (strict liability — intent doesn't matter) to release it or allow it to escape into the wild anywhere in the UK. Use secure, gnaw-proof caging; a trapped/escaped roof rat may NOT be released — only humane options or an exceptional licence apply.

Source: UK Government / legislation.gov.uk

In Great Britain, commercial breeding/selling (profit, >£1,000/yr, dealing, or systematic advertising) requires a local-authority Animal Welfare Activity Licence; expect possible 'Part I (non-domestic mammal)' treatment with specialist-knowledge + invasive-species containment requirements. In Northern Ireland, sale is prohibited entirely.
  • GB: apply to your local council for an Animal Activity Licence if you cross the business threshold
  • NI: do not sell/offer/transport-for-sale (Art. 15A)

Where: Local authority (GB); n/a (NI — prohibited) · Fees: Set by local authority

Source: Defra / local authorities, DAERA / legislation.gov.uk

Importing a roof rat needs an APHA Rabies Import Licence (Form RM01) — it's excluded from the Pet Travel Scheme. Non-EU origin = up to 4 months quarantine; EU origin may qualify for exemption if captive-bred and kept since birth. Apply to APHA Centre for International Trade (Carlisle) at least 4 weeks ahead.
  • Apply for APHA Form RM01 at least 4 weeks before import
  • Provide captive-bred-since-birth evidence to seek a quarantine exemption (EU origin)

Forms: APHA Rabies Import Licence (Form RM01) · Where: APHA Centre for International Trade, Carlisle · Fees: Quarantine at owner's expense

Source: APHA / UK Government

Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Japan

Summary. In Japan, keeping and hobby-breeding a captive-bred roof rat is legal and unregulated federally: the species is deliberately NOT a 'Specified Animal' (特定動物, hazardous) and NOT a 'Designated Invasive Alien Species' (特定外来生物) — a 2005 expert committee chose to exclude it because it's too long-established to regulate. Commercial activity (breeding for profit, retail sale, exhibition, or large-scale free rehoming) triggers registration as a First-Class (or Second-Class) Animal Handling Business with facility/welfare standards. The big restriction is IMPORT: bringing a roof rat into Japan is de-facto prohibited for the public — the Ministry of Health requires imported rodents to have lived since birth in a foreign-government-designated biosecure facility (homes/hobby breeders don't qualify). Never release one.

Cross-checked against official government sources.

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-07

Private possession needs no federal permit: R. rattus is not a 'Specified Animal' (特定動物 — that list targets primates, big carnivores, large/venomous reptiles, not rodents), and it is not a 'Designated Invasive Alien Species' (特定外来生物). The 2005 Ministry of the Environment expert committee deliberately excluded it (long-established via maritime trade; eradication-vs-pet distinction). Domestic keeping is treated like keeping a fancy rat or guinea pig.

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-07

Sources: Japan Ministry of the Environment (MOE)

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-07

Giving animals away free to 'a large number of unspecified people' on a continuing basis requires Second-Class (第二種) notification. Occasional free rehoming to friends/family is unregulated.

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-07

(R. rattus is not on the absolute-prohibition list, but the facility rule is an effective ban.) Export from Japan is legal with the destination country's health certificate (MAFF AQS). Never release.

  • Or file a Second-Class notification for large-scale free rehoming

Where: Prefectural government (animal welfare center / public health dept)

Source: Japan Ministry of the Environment (MOE), Japan Ministry of the Environment (MOE)

item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Netherlands

Summary. The black rat / roof rat (Rattus rattus) may not be acquired or kept as a pet in the Netherlands. Since 1 July 2024 the country operates a 'positive list' (huis- en hobbydierenlijst) under the Wet dieren and the Besluit huis- en hobbydierenlijst: only the ~31 mammal species named on the list may be kept, bred, bought, or sold without a permit. The brown rat (Rattus norvegicus, listed as the domesticated form) is on the list; Rattus rattus is not, so the default prohibition in Article 2.2 of the Wet dieren applies. A transitional arrangement (overgangsrecht, Article 3 of the Besluit) lets a person who demonstrably owned a Rattus rattus before 1 July 2024 keep that animal until its natural death, and transfer or transport it, provided reproduction is prevented and proof of pre-cutoff ownership passes with the animal. Breeding is prohibited for all non-listed species, including grandfathered animals. Importing a non-listed mammal is prohibited; export is not blocked by Dutch law. The list has a built-in pathway: any interested party may file an official species-assessment request (beoordeling aanvragen) with RVO to have a domesticated line of the species evaluated for addition.

Cross-checked against official government sources.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Restricted

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-13

Acquiring or keeping a black rat (Rattus rattus) as a new pet is prohibited: it is not on the positive list (huis- en hobbydierenlijst, in force since 1 July 2024), so the default ban in Article 2.2 of the Wet dieren applies (the brown rat, Rattus norvegicus, is listed; the black rat is not). The transitional arrangement (overgangsrecht, Art. 3 of the Besluit huis- en hobbydierenlijst) lets a person who demonstrably owned the specific animal before 1 July 2024 keep it until its natural death, on condition that reproduction is prevented and proof of pre-cutoff ownership (chip, dated receipt, old vet invoice, or EU pet passport) is held. Without such proof the keeping is unlawful and the animal can be seized. Classed as restricted because a lawful keeping pathway exists only for grandfathered animals; no new acquisition is permitted.

Sources: RVO (Netherlands), Overheid.nl (Dutch national law), NVWA (Netherlands), LICG (NL info centre)

Breeding   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-13

Breeding any mammal not on the positive list is prohibited, including Rattus rattus. The overgangsrecht (Art. 3 of the Besluit huis- en hobbydierenlijst) carries an absolute reproduction ban: a grandfathered animal may be kept only if reproduction is actively prevented (permanent single-sex housing, full separation of the sexes, or sterilisation/castration). Offspring are protected only in the narrow case of a pregnancy that demonstrably preceded 1 July 2024, and those offspring inherit the same breeding ban. Any pregnancy after the cutoff is unlawful, exposing the keeper to seizure of the parents and litter and administrative penalties.

Sources: Overheid.nl (Dutch national law), RVO (Netherlands), NVWA (Netherlands), LICG (NL info centre)

Selling or giving away   Restricted

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-13

There is no lawful trade in newly acquired black rats: the species cannot be bought or sold into the Netherlands because it is off the positive list. However, a legally grandfathered Rattus rattus (owned before 1 July 2024) may be sold, given away, or surrendered to a shelter, provided the proof of pre-cutoff ownership is transferred with the animal. The new keeper inherits the same status and the same absolute reproduction ban; if a recipient takes the animal without that documentation, they hold an illegal animal subject to enforcement. Commercial breeding/dealing in the species is effectively impossible because it cannot be lawfully acquired or bred.

Sources: Overheid.nl (Dutch national law), RVO (Netherlands), NVWA (Netherlands), LICG (NL info centre)

Transport & import   Restricted

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-13

Mixed. Internal transport within the Netherlands of a legally grandfathered Rattus rattus is unrestricted for legitimate purposes (relocation, transfer to a new keeper, veterinary visits). Import into the Netherlands of a non-listed mammal, whether from inside or outside the EU, is prohibited (the species lacks standing to enter for permanent keeping; the NVWA seizes such animals at border control posts under EU Reg. 2017/625). Export from the Netherlands is not blocked by Dutch law (the positive list has no extraterritorial reach), subject to the destination country's rules and the usual EU veterinary/health certification. Transit (doorvoer) through the country to a foreign destination where the species is legal is permitted under strict conditions. Never release a non-native into the wild (prohibited under the Omgevingswet / Bal art. 11.61).

Sources: NVWA (Netherlands), Overheid.nl (Dutch national law), LICG (NL info centre), NVWA (Netherlands)

Restrictions & responsibilities

Transitional arrangement (overgangsrecht): only an animal demonstrably owned before 1 July 2024 may be kept until its natural death, transferred, or transported. The keeper must hold proof of pre-cutoff ownership and prevent all reproduction. The proof must pass with the animal on any transfer, and the new keeper inherits the same conditions. Without proof, possession is unlawful and the animal can be seized.
  • Confirm the specific animal was demonstrably owned before 1 July 2024 (chip record, dated purchase/adoption receipt, old veterinary invoice, or EU pet passport dated before the cutoff)
  • Prevent reproduction permanently (single-sex housing, full separation of the sexes, or sterilisation/castration by a veterinarian)
  • On any transfer, pass the proof of pre-cutoff ownership to the new keeper, who inherits the same conditions
  • Do not acquire a new Rattus rattus and do not import one; never release it into the wild

Where: No filing required; retain documentation. Confirm evidentiary thresholds with RVO/NVWA.

Source: Overheid.nl (Dutch national law), RVO (Netherlands), LICG (NL info centre)

Import of a non-listed mammal (including Rattus rattus) into the Netherlands is prohibited and seized at the border by the NVWA; export is not blocked by Dutch law but must satisfy the destination country's rules plus the usual EU veterinary/health certification. Transit through the Netherlands to a foreign destination where the species is legal is allowed under strict, documented conditions.
  • Do not import a Rattus rattus into the Netherlands (border seizure under EU Reg. 2017/625)
  • For export, satisfy the destination country's import rules and obtain the required EU veterinary/health certificates
  • For transit, carry documents naming the foreign final destination and move efficiently via a recognised border point

Where: NVWA (border control / import-export certification)

Source: NVWA (Netherlands), NVWA (Netherlands)

It appears you can't currently keep a roof rat as a pet in Netherlands. Please confirm with the official sources above before acting. If you'd like to see this change, you can contact your representatives and the responsible agencies, ask them to treat a domesticated Rattus rattus line fairly and tell us what you learn so we can help others.

Help change this

How to help in Netherlands

Since 1 July 2024 the Netherlands has used a positive list for mammals, the huis- en hobbydierenlijst, under the Wet dieren and the Besluit huis- en hobbydierenlijst. A mammal species may only be kept, bred, bought, or sold without a permit if it is on that list. The list was built by scientifically assessing more than 300 species against six criteria. The brown rat (Rattus norvegicus, in its domesticated form) is on the list, so keeping domesticated brown rats is legal. The black rat / roof rat (Rattus rattus) is not on the list, so under the current rules a captive-bred, tame pet roof rat may not legally be acquired, kept, bred, or rehomed in the Netherlands, except under a narrow transitional arrangement for animals owned before 1 July 2024. The barrier is not an agency misreading the law; the law does not yet include this species. The framework is the Wet dieren (Article 2.2) and the Besluit huis- en hobbydierenlijst, administered by RVO (Rijksdienst voor Ondernemend Nederland) with enforcement by the NVWA. The already-permitted fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus) is itself the wild brown rat, domesticated only in the 19th century, so a captive-bred Rattus rattus is the same case one species over.

The ask: Ask RVO to assess a domesticated, captive-bred line of the black rat / roof rat (Rattus rattus) for addition to the huis- en hobbydierenlijst, using the official assessment procedure. The Dutch positive-list system has a built-in legal pathway: any interested party can submit a species-assessment request (beoordeling aanvragen) for an unlisted mammal through Mijn RVO. The brown rat is already on the list, which establishes that a domesticated Rattus species can meet the welfare criteria. The request is that the closely related, equally domesticable roof rat be evaluated on the same six-factor framework (human health, nutrition, habitat, thermoregulation, social behaviour and reproduction, and domestication). One of those six factors is domestication itself, and the framework already admits domesticated subspecies that would otherwise score too high. The relevant test is domestication, not wild ancestry. The dog descends from the wolf and the cat from a wild felid, yet both are recognised as domestic animals, because what counts is generations of captive breeding for tameness, not wild ancestry, and a captive-bred roof rat is domesticated in that same sense. The already-permitted fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus) is itself the wild brown rat, domesticated only in the 19th century, so a captive-bred Rattus rattus is the same case one species over (see https://blonderoofrat.com/how-the-sewer-rat-became-the-fancy-rat/ ). First, contact RVO's helpdesk to confirm the exact steps and the scientific documentation needed; then, if prepared to pursue it, file the formal assessment request (note the 500 euro fee per species).

Where the lever really is: The barrier is the law as written, specifically the species' absence from a statutory positive list. The Netherlands uses a verboden-tenzij (forbidden-unless) positive-list scheme under the Wet dieren and the Besluit huis- en hobbydierenlijst: only the ~31 mammal species on the huis- en hobbydierenlijst (in force since 1 July 2024) may be kept, bred, or traded. Rattus rattus is not on that list. RVO and the NVWA are applying the rule correctly when they say the roof rat may not be kept, so a complaint, an appeal, or a request to reinterpret the rule will not work, because nothing is being misread. The lever is to change what is on the list. The Dutch system does not require a legislative bill or a one-off public-comment window for this: the regulation contains its own standing assessment-request mechanism. Any belanghebbende (interested party) may file an official beoordeling aanvragen with RVO (via Mijn RVO, 500 euro per species, decision within 6 months, extendable to 9), supported by scientific sources on the assessment criteria, and the Adviescollege huis- en hobbydierenlijst evaluates the species for addition (risk classes A to F; A to C qualify, with domesticated subspecies admitted even where the wild form would not). That is the effective lever, and it is administrative rulemaking, not agency reinterpretation. The brown rat (Rattus norvegicus, domesticated form) is already on the list, which shows a domesticated Rattus line can satisfy the criteria, making the roof-rat case an evidence-driven extension rather than a novel claim.

Where to send it (more than one channel helps):

  • RVO (Rijksdienst voor Ondernemend Nederland) - general contact form / helpdesk for the huis- en hobbydierenlijst (executive / agency) — official contact page
    RVO administers the positive list and runs the assessment process. Use the helpdesk first to confirm exactly what an assessment request must contain and how an individual files it (DigiD via Mijn RVO). This is the right first touchpoint to understand the official pathway before committing the 500 euro application fee. Dutch-language form; RVO aims to reply within 3 working days. Phone: 088 042 47 47 (weekdays 08:30-17:00).
  • RVO - official species-assessment request portal (diersoort laten beoordelen / Mijn RVO) (public comment) — official contact page
    This is the statutory rulemaking lever: the official page describing how an interested party formally requests that a mammal species (here, Rattus rattus) be assessed for addition to the huis- en hobbydierenlijst. The actual request is submitted through Mijn RVO (DigiD login for individuals, eHerkenning for businesses), costs 500 euro per species, and gets a decision within 6 months (extendable to 9), evaluated by the Adviescollege huis- en hobbydierenlijst. This, not an appeal to the agency, is what can actually change the list.
  • NVWA (Nederlandse Voedsel- en Warenautoriteit) - enforcement authority, for status confirmation (executive / agency) — official contact page
    The NVWA enforces which animals may be kept and is the right place to confirm in writing the current keeping status of Rattus rattus and the documentary requirements of the overgangsrecht before you act. Useful as documentation, but note: the NVWA cannot add a species to the list, which is RVO's assessment process. Dutch-language web form.

A starting-point message — please put it in your own words; a short personal note carries far more weight than an identical form letter:

English
Subject: Request to assess the domesticated black rat (Rattus rattus) for the huis- en hobbydierenlijst

To the RVO team responsible for the huis- en hobbydierenlijst,

I am writing about a domesticated companion animal kept successfully elsewhere but not permitted in the Netherlands: the tame black rat / roof rat (Rattus rattus). I understand that since 1 July 2024 only mammal species on the huis- en hobbydierenlijst may be kept, and that Rattus rattus is not on it.

I request that a domesticated, captive-bred line of Rattus rattus be assessed for addition to the list. These animals are bred in captivity, tame and handleable, kept indoors as pets, and never released into the wild, like the brown rat (Rattus norvegicus, domesticated form), which is already on the list. The relevant question is the suitability of the kept, domesticated strain against your six assessment criteria, not the behaviour of wild populations. Domestication is itself one of those six criteria, and the framework already admits domesticated subspecies that the wild form would not reach. The relevant test is domestication, not wild ancestry. The dog descends from the wolf and the cat from a wild felid, yet both are recognised as domestic animals, because what defines a domestic animal is generations of captive breeding for tameness, not its species label. A captive-bred roof rat is domesticated in that same sense. The already-permitted brown rat (Rattus norvegicus) is itself the wild brown rat, domesticated only in the 19th century, so a captive-bred Rattus rattus is the same case one species over.

Please confirm the exact steps for submitting an assessment request (beoordeling aanvragen) for this species, and the scientific documentation the Adviescollege expects. I am prepared to pursue the formal application.

Thank you for your time.

[Your name]
[Your contact details]
Nederlands
Onderwerp: Verzoek tot beoordeling van de gedomesticeerde zwarte rat (Rattus rattus) voor de huis- en hobbydierenlijst

Geacht RVO-team verantwoordelijk voor de huis- en hobbydierenlijst,

Ik schrijf u over een gedomesticeerd gezelschapsdier dat elders met succes wordt gehouden, maar in Nederland niet gehouden mag worden: de tamme zwarte rat / dakrat (Rattus rattus). Ik begrijp dat sinds 1 juli 2024 alleen zoogdiersoorten op de huis- en hobbydierenlijst gehouden mogen worden, en dat Rattus rattus daar niet op staat.

Ik verzoek om een gedomesticeerde, in gevangenschap gefokte lijn van Rattus rattus te laten beoordelen voor opname op de lijst. Deze dieren worden in gevangenschap gefokt, zijn tam en hanteerbaar, worden binnenshuis als huisdier gehouden en worden nooit in het wild losgelaten, net als de bruine rat (Rattus norvegicus, gedomesticeerde vorm), die al op de lijst staat. De relevante vraag is de geschiktheid van de gehouden, gedomesticeerde lijn aan de hand van uw zes beoordelingscriteria, en niet het gedrag van wilde populaties. Domesticatie is zelf een van die zes criteria, en het beoordelingskader laat gedomesticeerde ondersoorten toe die in hun wilde vorm niet zouden worden toegelaten. Het relevante criterium is domesticatie, niet de wilde afstamming. De hond stamt af van de wolf en de kat van een wilde katachtige, en toch worden beide erkend als huisdieren, omdat een huisdier wordt bepaald door generaties van fokken in gevangenschap op tamheid en niet door de soortnaam. Een in gevangenschap gefokte zwarte rat is in diezelfde zin gedomesticeerd. De reeds toegestane bruine rat (Rattus norvegicus) is zelf de wilde bruine rat, pas in de 19e eeuw gedomesticeerd, zodat een in gevangenschap gefokte Rattus rattus hetzelfde geval is, een soort verder.

Kunt u mij bevestigen wat de exacte stappen zijn om een beoordeling aan te vragen voor deze soort, en welke wetenschappelijke onderbouwing het Adviescollege verwacht? Ik ben bereid de formele aanvraag in te dienen.

Met vriendelijke groet,

[Uw naam]
[Uw contactgegevens]

Did you take action, or get a response? Tell us — it helps the next person, and we track what actually works.

item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › New Zealand

Summary. New Zealand treats the ship rat (Rattus rattus) as an invasive pest, not a permissible companion animal. It is managed as an unwanted organism under the Biosecurity Act 1993 and is a primary target of the national Predator Free 2050 eradication programme; under the Wildlife Act 1953 it is unprotected wildlife (Schedule 5). The Ministry for Primary Industries (MPI) confirmed in writing (June 2026) that pet rats cannot be imported into New Zealand, so import is prohibited. Within the country, Biosecurity Act section 53 prohibits breeding, propagating, selling, offering for sale, or exhibiting an unwanted organism, and section 52 prohibits its release or spread, so breeding and sale/transfer of a ship rat are prohibited. The Act does not list mere possession among its prohibited activities, so passive keeping of an already-present, securely contained animal sits in a narrow tolerated space, but the owner bears strict liability for any escape and regional pest-management plans can compel removal; the species has no recognised domestication exemption (the pet kept lawfully in New Zealand is the fancy rat, Rattus norvegicus). Never release any rat.

Key points here are confirmed in writing by the responsible agency (see below).
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
Confirmed by the agencies.
  • Ministry for Primary Industries (MPI), Animal Welfare Team, written reply June 2026: there are NO registration or permit requirements under the Animal Welfare Act 1999 for people keeping, breeding, or selling rats (only the Act's general welfare duties and codes of welfare apply; there is no pet-rat-specific code of welfare). MPI also confirmed that pet rats CANNOT be imported into New Zealand (per MPI's 'Bringing pets to NZ other than cats and dogs' guidance). Note: this welfare-team reply addressed only the Animal Welfare Act layer; it did not address the Biosecurity Act 1993 status of the ship rat (Rattus rattus) specifically, which is the controlling framework and treats the species as an unwanted organism.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Restricted

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-13

There is no Animal Welfare Act 1999 registration or permit to keep a rat (MPI, June 2026), and the Biosecurity Act 1993 does not list mere possession among the activities it prohibits for an unwanted organism (section 53 names selling, exhibiting, propagating, breeding, and multiplying; section 52 names release and spread). Passive keeping of an already-present, securely contained ship rat therefore sits in a narrow tolerated space rather than being outright banned. However, it is not freely permitted: Rattus rattus is managed as an unwanted organism and is a Predator Free 2050 eradication target, the owner bears strict liability under section 52 if the animal escapes (an escape is the release of an unwanted organism), and regional pest-management plans can require its removal. The domestication tolerance extended in practice to the fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus) is not a statutory exemption and does not clearly cover Rattus rattus. Acquiring one lawfully is in any case blocked because import is prohibited and breeding and sale are prohibited.

Sources: New Zealand Legislation (Parliamentary Counsel Office), Ministry for Primary Industries (MPI), NZ Department of Conservation, New Zealand Legislation (Parliamentary Counsel Office), New Zealand Legislation (Parliamentary Counsel Office)

Breeding   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-13

Section 53(1)(c) of the Biosecurity Act 1993 provides that a person in charge of an organism they know or suspect to be an unwanted organism must not propagate, breed, or multiply it, or otherwise act in a manner likely to encourage its propagation. Rattus rattus is managed as an unwanted organism, so breeding it is prohibited. A Chief Technical Officer may permit an otherwise-prohibited act under section 53(2), but in practice such permissions are confined to education, research, and pest-management purposes and are not granted for hobby or companion-animal breeding. The absence of an Animal Welfare Act breeding permit (MPI, June 2026) does not change this; the welfare framework and the Biosecurity framework are separate, and the Biosecurity prohibition controls.

Sources: New Zealand Legislation (Parliamentary Counsel Office), Ministry for Primary Industries (MPI), NZ Department of Conservation

Selling or giving away   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-13

Section 53(1) of the Biosecurity Act 1993 prohibits a person in charge of an unwanted organism from causing or permitting it to be in a place where organisms are offered for sale or exhibited, and from selling or offering it for sale. Transferring a ship rat (by sale or by gift) is therefore prohibited, because Rattus rattus is managed as an unwanted organism and any transfer risks its spread and propagation. There is no separate pet-dealer licence that can bypass this, and no small-breeder or hobby exemption. The Animal Welfare Act imposes no dealer permit (MPI, June 2026), but that welfare-layer answer does not displace the Biosecurity prohibition.

Sources: New Zealand Legislation (Parliamentary Counsel Office), Ministry for Primary Industries (MPI), NZ Department of Conservation

Transport & import   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-13

Importing a roof rat into New Zealand is prohibited. MPI confirmed in writing (June 2026) that pet rats cannot be imported, and its 'Bringing pets to NZ (other than cats and dogs)' guidance does not provide any pathway for rats; live rodents enter only via a tightly controlled research/laboratory pathway (a section 52/53 unwanted-organisms permission plus an import health standard, routed to an approved transitional containment facility), which is not available for private pets. Domestic movement of a ship rat is also restricted: section 52 of the Biosecurity Act prohibits releasing or spreading an unwanted organism, and regional pest-management plans bar moving rats into controlled areas such as the Hauraki Gulf Controlled Area near pest-free islands. Any internal movement of a lawfully held animal must also meet the Animal Welfare (Transport within New Zealand) Code of Welfare. Never release any rat.

Sources: Ministry for Primary Industries (MPI), New Zealand Legislation (Parliamentary Counsel Office), Ministry for Primary Industries (MPI), Auckland Council

Restrictions & responsibilities

Pet rats cannot be imported into New Zealand (MPI, June 2026). There is no import pathway for a roof rat from any country; live rodents are admitted only through a research/laboratory pathway (a Chief Technical Officer unwanted-organisms permission under Biosecurity Act ss 52/53 plus an import health standard, routed to an approved transitional containment facility), which is not available for private pets. Domestic movement is also restricted: do not move a rat into a controlled area such as the Hauraki Gulf Controlled Area, and meet the Animal Welfare (Transport within New Zealand) Code of Welfare for any internal transport. Never release any rat.
  • Do not attempt to import a roof rat into New Zealand - there is no pet pathway
  • Treat the research/laboratory import pathway (CTO permission + import health standard + transitional facility) as unavailable for a companion animal
  • Do not move any rat into a controlled area such as the Hauraki Gulf Controlled Area
  • For any lawful internal transport, meet the Animal Welfare (Transport within New Zealand) Code of Welfare
  • Never release a rat into the environment - it is a Predator Free 2050 eradication target

Where: Ministry for Primary Industries (MPI) - Biosecurity New Zealand / Animal Imports

Source: Ministry for Primary Industries (MPI), New Zealand Legislation (Parliamentary Counsel Office), Auckland Council

The ship rat is managed as an unwanted organism under the Biosecurity Act 1993. Section 53 prohibits propagating, breeding, multiplying, selling, offering for sale, or exhibiting it, so breeding and sale/gifting are prohibited. Section 52 prohibits releasing or spreading it, so any escape of a kept animal is itself an offence (strict liability). A Chief Technical Officer can permit an otherwise-prohibited act under ss 52/53, but in practice only for education, research, or pest management, not for companion-animal keeping. Regional pest-management plans can require removal of the species on private land. There is no recognised domestication exemption for Rattus rattus.
  • Understand that breeding and selling/gifting a ship rat are prohibited under Biosecurity Act s 53
  • Understand that an escape is the release of an unwanted organism (s 52) and the keeper is strictly liable
  • Do not assume the practical tolerance shown to the fancy rat (R. norvegicus) extends to R. rattus - it has no statutory domestication exemption
  • If a research/education/pest-management purpose genuinely applies, seek a Chief Technical Officer permission from MPI before acting (not available for pet keeping)

Where: Ministry for Primary Industries (MPI) - Biosecurity New Zealand

Source: New Zealand Legislation (Parliamentary Counsel Office), Ministry for Primary Industries (MPI), NZ Department of Conservation

Keepers of any animal owe the Animal Welfare Act 1999 duties (meet the animal's physical, health, and behavioural needs and provide treatment for sickness or injury); breaching a minimum standard in a code of welfare can support a prosecution. There is no code of welfare specific to pet rats, but the general duties apply. This welfare duty is separate from, and additional to, the Biosecurity Act controls on the ship rat.

Source: New Zealand Legislation (Parliamentary Counsel Office)

It appears you can't currently keep a roof rat as a pet in New Zealand. Please confirm with the official sources above before acting. If you'd like to see this change, you can contact your representatives and the responsible agencies, ask them to treat a domesticated Rattus rattus line fairly and tell us what you learn so we can help others.

item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Sweden

Summary. Sweden is permissive for the roof rat — now confirmed in writing by the Swedish Board of Agriculture (Jordbruksverket, June 2026). There is no species-specific ban: R. rattus is not on the EU invasive-species Union list (Reg. 1143/2014) and not on Sweden's national invasive list (Förordning 2026:311). The Animal Welfare Act (Djurskyddslagen 2018:1192) regulates HOW animals are kept, not WHICH rodent species, and the Board of Agriculture's rules (SJVFS 2019:15) cover rats generically as gnagare. Jordbruksverket confirmed it is permitted to keep R. rattus as pets as long as they are not wild-caught, with NO permit and NO registration; only PROFESSIONAL (yrkesmässig) keeping/breeding/selling needs to check with the county board (länsstyrelsen) — larger-scale but non-professional hobby activity is EXEMPT from the permit requirement (except breeding animals intended as feeder/feed animals). Welfare and enclosure standards apply (SJVFS 2019:15 ch. 1; enclosure size/enrichment per SJVFS 2019:29 ch. 11 §§17-18). Ironically R. rattus is classed as EXTINCT (RE) in the wild in Sweden, so captive pets pose essentially zero invasion risk. Cross-border transport of pet rodents needs no registration (commercial transport requires authorisation as an animal transporter); intra-EU commercial movement, or more than 5 pet animals, needs an Article 151 Animal Health Law self-declaration from a registered establishment — no TRACES notification and no health certificate. Non-EU import is tighter.

Key points here are confirmed in writing by the responsible agency (see below).
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
Confirmed by the agencies.
  • Swedish Board of Agriculture (Jordbruksverket), written reply June 2026: it is permitted to keep Rattus rattus as pets in Sweden as long as the animals are not caught in the wild, with NO permit and NO registration required (SJVFS 2019:15, ch. 1 §§4-5). Welfare and enclosure-size/enrichment standards apply (SJVFS 2019:15 ch. 1; SJVFS 2019:29 ch. 11 §§17-18). A permit is only relevant for PROFESSIONAL (yrkesmässig) keeping, breeding, or selling — larger-scale but non-professional hobby activity is exempt (except breeding animals intended as feeder/feed animals); professional operators should ask their county administrative board (länsstyrelsen) whether a permit is needed. Cross-border transport of pet rodents needs no registration; commercial transport requires authorisation as an animal transporter, and intra-EU commercial movement (or more than 5 pet animals) needs an Article 151 Animal Health Law self-declaration from a registered establishment — no TRACES notification and no health certificate. The agency also confirmed the '6 enclosures' figure refers to the number of cages.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

Jordbruksverket confirmed (June 2026) it is permitted to keep R. rattus as pets as long as they are not wild-caught, with no permit and no registration (SJVFS 2019:15 ch. 1 §§4-5). Djurskyddslagen 2018:1192 imposes welfare duties but no species ban; R. rattus is absent from the EU Union list and Sweden's national invasive list (Förordning 2026:311). Keepers must meet welfare/enclosure standards (SJVFS 2019:15 ch. 1; enclosure size/furnishing/enrichment per SJVFS 2019:29 ch. 11 §§17-18) and the social-species rule (keep ≥2 rats).

Sources: Sveriges Riksdag, Statens jordbruksverk, Sveriges Riksdag / Naturvårdsverket, EU / EUR-Lex

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

Jordbruksverket confirmed (June 2026) that keeping, breeding, or selling pets other than dogs and cats at larger scale but NOT in a professional manner is EXEMPT from the permit requirement — so a private/hobby rattery needs no permit regardless of cage count. Only PROFESSIONAL (yrkesmässig) breeding must ask the county administrative board (länsstyrelsen) whether a permit is required, and the exemption does NOT cover breeding animals intended to be sold as feeder/feed animals. (The agency clarified the '6 enclosures' figure refers to the number of cages.) Welfare standards apply throughout.

Sources: Sveriges Riksdag, Statens jordbruksverk, Statens jordbruksverk

Selling or giving away   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

Free transfers and sales between hobbyists are permit-free: Jordbruksverket confirmed (June 2026) that larger-scale but non-professional keeping/breeding/selling of pets other than dogs and cats is exempt from the permit requirement (Sweden has no separate pet-shop licence). Only PROFESSIONAL (yrkesmässig) selling must check with the county administrative board (länsstyrelsen). SJVFS 2019:15 sets sale conditions (health checks, documentation). No species ban or price cap on captive-bred R. rattus; the exemption excludes breeding animals sold as feeder/feed animals.

Sources: Sveriges Riksdag, Statens jordbruksverk

Transport & import   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

Jordbruksverket confirmed (June 2026): cross-border transport of pet rodents needs NO registration. If animals are moved in connection with an economic activity, the carrier must be authorised as an animal transporter (SJVFS 2019:7; minimum rodent-container requirements in Annex/Bilaga 1.11). For intra-EU COMMERCIAL movement, or movement of more than 5 pet animals, no health certificate and no TRACES notification are required, but an Article 151 Animal Health Law (Reg. 2016/429) self-declaration is — issued by the operator at the place of origin, which must itself be registered as an establishment for terrestrial animals (Art. 84). There is no numeric cap on a single commercial movement and no fixed template for the self-declaration. Non-EU import follows different, tighter rules. Internal transport is unregulated beyond welfare. Never release.

Sources: Jordbruksverket, EU / EUR-Lex

Restrictions & responsibilities

Only PROFESSIONAL (yrkesmässig) keeping, breeding, or selling of pet rodents needs to check with your county administrative board (länsstyrelsen) about a permit — larger-scale but non-professional hobby activity is EXEMPT (Jordbruksverket, June 2026), except breeding animals intended to be sold as feeder/feed animals, which is not exempt. Transport in connection with an economic activity requires authorisation as an animal transporter (SJVFS 2019:7). Meet the welfare rules (minimum enclosure size, enrichment, and keep rats in groups of ≥2). Never release a roof rat.
  • If operating professionally, ask your länsstyrelsen whether a permit is required
  • For transport in connection with an economic activity, register as an authorised animal transporter with Jordbruksverket

Where: Länsstyrelsen (county administrative board); Jordbruksverket for transporter authorisation

Source: Statens jordbruksverk, Statens jordbruksverk

  • SJVFS 2019:15 — conditions for keeping/breeding/selling companion & hobby animals (covers rats/gnagare) — Statens jordbruksverk
