item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Singapore? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Singapore

Summary. Singapore prohibits the roof rat as a pet, completely. It runs a closed 'positive list': only species the Animal & Veterinary Service (AVS, a cluster under the National Parks Board) has approved may be kept. The approved small-mammal list includes the domestic mouse (Mus musculus) alongside rabbits, hamsters, guinea pigs, gerbils and chinchillas — but NO species of the genus Rattus, so neither the roof rat (R. rattus) nor the ordinary fancy rat (R. norvegicus) may be kept. Because it is not a listed pet, R. rattus defaults to 'wildlife' under the Wildlife Act 1965, and s.5C(1) makes it a strict-liability offence to keep any wildlife without the Director-General's written approval (no such approval is available to the public). Breeding is separately barred by the Control of Vectors and Pesticides Act 1998 (CVPA), which defines any rodent 'capable of carrying' disease as a public-health vector and, under s.16, prohibits breeding vectors without permission; sale/transfer is blocked by the Wildlife Act (s.8) and the AVS pet-shop licensing rules (the hobbyist breeding exemption applies only to approved 'relevant pet animals'). The ONLY lawful pathway for any Rattus is institutional: an accredited Animal Research Facility (ARF) may import and keep lab rats — never a private pet keeper. One statutory quirk: the Wildlife (Exemption) Order 2020 cull-list names R. norvegicus and R. tanezumi (and Mus musculus castaneus, Suncus murinus) as exempt from the s.5C culling ban, but R. rattus is omitted, so a strict reading paradoxically gives the wild roof rat unpermitted-culling protection denied its cousins — an anomaly that offers a pet keeper nothing. Not CITES-listed; the closed positive list, not CITES, is the operative bar.

Cross-checked against official government sources.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-12

R. rattus is not on the AVS approved-pet positive list (which permits mice, rabbits, hamsters, guinea pigs, gerbils, chinchillas — no Rattus), so it defaults to 'wildlife' under the Wildlife Act 1965. Section 5C(1) provides that 'a person must not intentionally kill, trap, take or keep any wildlife in any place unless the person has the Director-General's written approval to do so' — a strict-liability offence (belief that the animal is a domesticated pet is no defence), carrying up to S$20,000 fine and/or 12 months' imprisonment for a first offence. The Wildlife Act's domestic-animal carve-outs (dogs, cats, livestock, poultry) do not include any rat, and no public permit/registration pathway exists to keep a roof rat. AVS guidance also treats rats as vermin that will not be allowed.

Sources: Singapore Statutes Online / Attorney-General's Chambers; administered by NParks, Animal & Veterinary Service (AVS), NParks, Singapore Statutes Online / AGC; administered by AVS (NParks)

Breeding   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-12

Breeding is interdicted by public-health law independent of the keeping ban. The Control of Vectors and Pesticides Act 1998 (CVPA) s.2 defines a 'vector' to include 'any rodent, including its young, which is carrying or causing, or capable of carrying or causing, any disease to human beings' — the test is the species' biological capacity, so a captive-bred, pathogen-free R. rattus is still a vector. CVPA s.16 ('Prohibition on breeding, etc., of vectors without Director-General's permission') makes it a strict criminal offence to intentionally breed vectors; no private hobbyist permit is ever issued (penalties under s.23 run to large fines and imprisonment). The only entities permitted to breed Rattus are licensed Animal Research Facilities. Keeping the animal to breed it is independently barred under the Wildlife Act s.5C, so a hobbyist breeding programme is doubly unlawful.

Sources: Singapore Statutes Online / AGC; administered by NEA, Singapore Statutes Online / Attorney-General's Chambers; administered by NParks

Selling or giving away   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-12

Sale or transfer (including giving away free) is blocked on two layers. (1) Wildlife Act 1965 s.8 prohibits selling, offering for sale, or exporting any wildlife without the Director-General's written approval; doing so in the course of an animal-related business is aggravated (s.5C(3)(b)(i): up to S$20,000 / 12 months even on a first offence). (2) The Animals and Birds (Licensing of Premises for Pet Shop and Other Purposes) Rules require an AVS pet-shop/breeding licence to distribute, breed, exhibit or sell pet animals (Rule 4), and AVS will not licence the sale of a non-positive-listed species. The Schedule 1 hobbyist 'breed-and-give-away-for-adoption' exemption applies only to a 'relevant pet animal or bird' — which excludes all Rattus — so it is legally void for the roof rat. Therefore one cannot lawfully sell, trade, or give away a roof rat in Singapore.

Sources: Singapore Statutes Online / Attorney-General's Chambers; administered by NParks, Singapore Statutes Online / AGC; administered by AVS, Animal & Veterinary Service (AVS), NParks

Transport & import   Restricted

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-12

Import/export of animals requires an AVS import licence under the Animals and Birds Act 1965 s.7 (no person may import any animal without the Director-General's licence). The framework bifurcates rodents into two mutually exclusive paths. PERSONAL PET import is allowed only for positive-listed small mammals — the AVS pet-import page lists rabbits, mice, hamsters, gerbils, guinea pigs and chinchillas, and the GoBusiness licensing system summarily rejects a personal pet application for any Rattus species; so personal import/transport of a roof rat is effectively PROHIBITED. The ONLY lawful pathway is institutional: an accredited Animal Research Facility (ARF) licensed under the Animals and Birds (Care and Use of Animals for Scientific Purposes) Rules may import lab 'rats' from an AVS-approved overseas facility, with a commercial veterinary health certificate, pre-arrival border inspection (≥5 days' notice) and quarantine (import licence ~S$174 express). That route is closed to private citizens. Not CITES-listed. Never release.

Sources: Singapore Statutes Online / AGC; administered by AVS (NParks), Animal & Veterinary Service (AVS), NParks, Animal & Veterinary Service (AVS), NParks

Restrictions & responsibilities

The roof rat cannot lawfully be kept, bred, sold, given away, or imported as a pet in Singapore. No Rattus species is on the AVS approved-pet positive list (only the mouse, Mus musculus, among small rodents), so the roof rat is 'wildlife' under the Wildlife Act 1965 — keeping it without the Director-General's written approval is a strict-liability offence under s.5C (up to S$20,000 / 12 months), breeding it is barred as a public-health 'vector' under CVPA 1998 s.16, and selling/transferring it is barred under Wildlife Act s.8 and the AVS pet-shop licensing rules. The ban is genus-wide (the ordinary fancy rat R. norvegicus is barred too). There is no private permit, licence, or hobbyist exemption. Never release.
  • Do not keep, breed, sell, give away, or import a roof rat in Singapore — no private permit pathway exists (Wildlife Act s.5C; CVPA s.16; Animals and Birds Act / pet-shop rules)
  • Never release a roof rat (it is a documented public-health vector and pest)

Where: Animal & Veterinary Service (AVS), National Parks Board

Source: Singapore Statutes Online / Attorney-General's Chambers; administered by NParks, Singapore Statutes Online / AGC; administered by NEA, Singapore Statutes Online / AGC; administered by AVS (NParks), Animal & Veterinary Service (AVS), NParks

The only lawful route by which any Rattus may be imported, bred or kept in Singapore is institutional research. An accredited Animal Research Facility (ARF) licensed under the Animals and Birds (Care and Use of Animals for Scientific Purposes) Rules — with an Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC), an attending veterinarian and AVS oversight — may import lab rats from an AVS-approved overseas facility under a commercial veterinary health certificate, with pre-arrival border inspection (≥5 days' notice) and quarantine. This pathway is closed to private individuals and confers no private pet-keeping right.
  • (Institutions only) Hold a valid AVS Animal Research Facility (ARF) licence with an IACUC and attending veterinarian
  • Import lab rats only from an AVS-accredited overseas facility, with a commercial veterinary health certificate
  • Book border-control inspection at least 5 days before arrival; complete inspection and quarantine on arrival

Forms: AVS — Importing and exporting laboratory animals, GoBusiness — Licence for Animal Research Facility · Where: Animal & Veterinary Service (AVS), NParks (ARF licence + import licence via GoBusiness) · Fees: Import licence for non-food animals/biologics ~S$174 (express, issued one working day after submission)

Source: Animal & Veterinary Service (AVS), NParks, Singapore Statutes Online / AGC; administered by AVS

It appears you can't currently keep a roof rat as a pet in Singapore. Please confirm with the official sources above before acting. If you'd like to see this change, you can contact your representatives and the responsible agencies, ask them to treat a domesticated Rattus rattus line fairly and tell us what you learn so we can help others.

Official sources

  • Wildlife Act 1965 (2020 Revised Edition) — s.5C (no keeping/killing/trapping/taking wildlife without Director-General approval), s.8 (sale/export of wildlife), s.2 'wildlife' definition, s.6 'defence of property' — Singapore Statutes Online / Attorney-General's Chambers; administered by NParks
  • Animals and Birds Act 1965 — prevention of epizootic disease; s.7 import licence; premises licensing power — Singapore Statutes Online / AGC; administered by AVS (NParks)
  • Control of Vectors and Pesticides Act 1998 — s.2 'vector' (rodent capable of carrying disease), s.16 (prohibition on breeding vectors without Director-General permission), s.23 (penalties) — Singapore Statutes Online / AGC; administered by NEA
  • Wildlife (Exemption) Order 2020 — Schedule exempts R. norvegicus, R. tanezumi, Mus musculus castaneus, Suncus murinus from the s.5C culling ban; R. rattus omitted — Singapore Statutes Online / AGC; made under Wildlife Act 1965
  • Animals and Birds (Licensing of Premises for Pet Shop and Other Purposes) Rules — Rule 4 (pet-shop/breeding licence to distribute/breed/exhibit/sell) + Schedule 1 (hobbyist exemption limited to a 'relevant pet animal or bird') — Singapore Statutes Online / AGC; administered by AVS
  • Animals and Birds (Care and Use of Animals for Scientific Purposes) Rules — Animal Research Facility (ARF) licensing for laboratory animals — Singapore Statutes Online / AGC; administered by AVS
  • AVS — Animals that can be kept as pets (approved positive list: rabbits, mice, hamsters, guinea pigs, gerbils, chinchillas; no Rattus) — Animal & Veterinary Service (AVS), NParks
  • AVS — Importing small mammals (personal pet import allowed only for approved species: rabbits, mice, hamsters, gerbils, guinea pigs, chinchillas; AVS import licence + quarantine) — Animal & Veterinary Service (AVS), NParks
  • AVS — Importing and exporting laboratory animals (lab 'rats' permitted only for accredited Animal Research Facilities; commercial health certificate, border inspection, quarantine) — Animal & Veterinary Service (AVS), NParks

item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States

Summary. Under U.S. federal law, KEEPING a roof rat as a pet is unregulated (left to the states). But the common belief that all rats are federally exempt is wrong for Rattus rattus: the Animal Welfare Act's rat exclusion covers only research-bred rats, so commercial BREEDERS and SELLERS can need a USDA license (small hobby breeders and face-to-face sales/giveaways are exempt), and because the USFWS classifies Rattus rattus as 'wildlife,' IMPORTING or EXPORTING one requires a Form 3-177 wildlife declaration even for a captive-bred pet.

Cross-checked against official government sources.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

The federal government does not regulate private, non-commercial possession of pet rats; under the Tenth Amendment this is left to state, county, and municipal law. Rattus rattus is not federally listed as injurious or endangered, so nothing federal stops you from keeping one (your state/city may).

Sources: U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service, USFWS

Breeding   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

Pet roof rats are NOT exempt from the Animal Welfare Act (its exclusion covers only rats 'bred for use in research,' 7 U.S.C. 2132(g); 9 C.F.R. 1.1), so they are regulated 'animals.' But a USDA license is needed ONLY if you sell the offspring WHOLESALE (to resellers) or SIGHT-UNSEEN (shipped to a buyer who has not seen the animal). Selling or placing rats face-to-face to the final owner, or giving them away, is exempt as a 'retail' transaction with NO limit on the number of breeding females (9 C.F.R. 2.1(a)(3)). The 'four or fewer breeding females' exemption only matters for sight-unseen/shipped sales.

Sources: USDA-APHIS / U.S. Code, USDA-APHIS

Selling or giving away   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

A USDA Class B dealer license is required only for WHOLESALE sales (to resellers/pet stores) or SIGHT-UNSEEN shipped sales. Selling face-to-face to the final owner (a 'retail pet store' transaction, which includes a home breeder selling directly), and giving rats away, are exempt — with NO limit on the number of breeding females (9 C.F.R. 1.1, 2.1(a)(3)). Only a wholesale or sight-unseen seller keeping 5 or more breeding females must be licensed.

Sources: USDA-APHIS / U.S. Code, USDA-APHIS

Transport & import   Restricted

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

Moving a roof rat between U.S. states needs no federal permit (and since U.S. v. Zinke (2017) even injurious species may move between contiguous states), BUT the Lacey Act (16 U.S.C. 3372) makes it a federal crime to transport one into a state where it is illegal. IMPORT/EXPORT is more involved: the USFWS classifies Rattus rattus as 'wildlife' (only Rattus norvegicus is on the domesticated-exemption list, 50 C.F.R. 14.4), so each shipment needs a USFWS Form 3-177 declaration, entry/exit through a designated wildlife port, and an inspection fee, even for a captive-bred pet (the personal-pet exemption waives only the commercial license). The CDC African-rodent import ban (42 C.F.R. 71.56) does not apply to roof rats sourced outside Africa, and USDA Veterinary Services has no health requirements for pet-rodent import.

Restrictions & responsibilities

A USDA APHIS license (Class A breeder / Class B dealer) is required ONLY for WHOLESALE selling or SIGHT-UNSEEN shipping by someone keeping 5 or more breeding females. Selling face-to-face to the final owner, or giving rats away, is EXEMPT no matter how many breeding females you keep (the 'retail pet store' exemption, 9 CFR 2.1(a)(3)).
  • Check whether you exceed the exemption thresholds (9 CFR 2.1(a)(3))
  • If not exempt, apply for the appropriate USDA license and meet the 9 CFR Part 3 housing/care standards

Forms: USDA AWA licensing rule & exemptions (9 CFR 2.1) · Where: USDA APHIS Animal Care · Fees: Varies by license type/size

Source: USDA-APHIS, USDA-APHIS / U.S. Code

Importing or exporting a roof rat requires a USFWS wildlife declaration (Form 3-177), clearance at a designated wildlife port, and a per-shipment inspection fee, because Rattus rattus is legally 'wildlife' (it is not on the 50 CFR 14.4 domesticated list). The personal-pet exemption waives only the commercial Import/Export license, not the declaration, port, or inspection.

  • Route the shipment through a designated wildlife port (or get a Designated Port Exception Permit)

Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Canada › Alberta

Summary. Alberta is the strictest jurisdiction in Canada — and one of the strictest anywhere. Under the Agricultural Pests Act and the Pest and Nuisance Control Regulation, the ENTIRE genus Rattus is a declared pest, and the law prohibits the import, purchase, sale, transport, and possession of any live rat. There is NO exemption for 'fancy', tame, or captive-bred rats. The only legal route is a special Ministerial permit reserved for accredited research institutions, zoos, or approved labs. A pet roof rat in Alberta may be seized and destroyed, and the keeper fined. Alberta has defended its 'rat-free' status since 1950.

Cross-checked against official government sources.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
National law also applies. These are the Alberta-specific rules; Canada’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where Alberta is silent. See Canada.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

The Agricultural Pests Act declares the whole genus Rattus a pest, and possession of a live rat by a private citizen is unlawful — Alberta enforces a zero-tolerance 'rat-free' policy. There is explicitly no exemption for fancy, tame, or domesticated rats; a single caged pet is treated as an unacceptable escape risk. Wild sightings are reported to the 310-RATS line and eradicated.

Sources: Government of Alberta, Government of Alberta, Government of Alberta

Breeding   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

Breeding requires possession, which is prohibited, and the statute separately forbids the purchase, sale, or distribution of a declared pest. There is no legal hobby or commercial breeding of rats in Alberta.

Sources: Government of Alberta, Government of Alberta

Selling or giving away   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

Selling, giving, or otherwise distributing a live rat is expressly prohibited as dealing in a declared pest. No pet-trade layer exists for rats in Alberta.

Sources: Government of Alberta, Government of Alberta

Transport & import   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

Transporting a live rat into or within Alberta is prohibited except under a highly restricted Ministerial permit (research institutions, zoos, approved labs only). Whether a non-resident may drive a securely caged pet rat continuously THROUGH Alberta without stopping is not clearly addressed in the published rules — we have asked the province to clarify. Treat any presence of a rat in Alberta as prohibited unless you hold a permit.

Sources: Government of Alberta, Government of Alberta

Restrictions & responsibilities

The only lawful way to possess, breed, or transport a rat in Alberta is a special permit issued by the Minister of Agriculture, available only to accredited research institutions, major zoos, or government-approved laboratories — not to private pet keepers.
  • Pet keeping is not permitted — there is no pet-owner permit

Where: Alberta Agriculture and Irrigation (Ministerial permit)

Source: Government of Alberta, Government of Alberta

If you move to Alberta, you cannot bring a pet rat with you. Rehome it responsibly before relocating; do not transport it into the province. Rat sightings are reported to 310-RATS (310-7287) and acted on.

Source: Government of Alberta

Alberta's only legal route to hold any Rattus is a Ministerial Form-6 permit (AR 184/2001 s.11) limited to research facilities, zoos, and inspectors — no private/hobby pathway. Even the fancy rat (R. norvegicus) is prohibited for private keeping.

Forms: AR 184/2001 Form 6 — Ministerial permit to keep rats (research/zoo/inspector only) · Where: Alberta Agriculture and Irrigation — Inspection and Investigation Section

It appears you can't currently keep a roof rat as a pet in Alberta. Please confirm with the official sources above before acting. If you'd like to see this change, you can contact your representatives and the responsible agencies, ask them to treat a domesticated Rattus rattus line fairly and tell us what you learn so we can help others.

Help change this

How to help in Alberta

Alberta is one of the only places with a total ban on keeping any pet rat. Under the Agricultural Pests Act (RSA 2000, c. A-8) and the Pest and Nuisance Control Regulation (AR 184/2001), the entire genus Rattus, every rat species including the tame fancy pet rat (Rattus norvegicus) and the roof rat (Rattus rattus), is a declared agricultural pest. The Government of Alberta states that it is illegal to own pet rats in Alberta. Possession, import, purchase, sale, transport, and breeding of any live rat are all prohibited. The only permit (a Ministerial permit under AR 184/2001) is reserved for accredited research institutions, zoos, and government labs; there is no private or hobby pathway, not even for a single captive-bred, tame rat kept indoors in a cage. Penalties can reach $5,000 per animal, and a pet rat found in the province can be seized and destroyed. The ban is the backbone of Alberta's 75-year rat-free status, and it makes no distinction between a wild invasive rat and a domesticated companion animal that has never lived outdoors.

The ask: Ask the Legislative Assembly (your MLA) to amend the Agricultural Pests Act and Pest and Nuisance Control Regulation to create a narrow, well-defined exemption for domesticated, captive-bred pet rats kept indoors under reasonable conditions (for example: spayed or neutered or single-sex housing, secure escape-proof caging, microchipping or registration, and a ban on outdoor release), distinct from Alberta's wild-rat eradication program, which would continue unchanged. Do not ask the rat-control program or Alberta Agriculture to make an exception, because that office is correctly applying a law it cannot rewrite. The change has to come from the Legislature.

Where the lever really is: Branch (b): the problem is the law as written, not a bureaucracy misreading it. The Agricultural Pests Act and AR 184/2001 declare the whole genus Rattus a pest at the statutory and regulatory level, and the rat-control agency is correctly applying that prohibition; the Government of Alberta's website confirms that it is illegal to own pet rats in Alberta. There is no exemption list a tame or captive-bred rat could be added to, and the sole permit category is statutorily confined to research, zoo, and lab operators. Appealing to the agency (rats@gov.ab.ca / 310-FARM) will not change anything: that line exists to report and eradicate rats, and the staff have no authority to legalize pet keeping. The only lever that can change this is the Legislature, by amending the Act or the Regulation to carve out a domesticated-pet-rat exemption, which means writing to your MLA and, where relevant, the Minister of Agriculture and Irrigation in their legislative and policy capacity. The single narrow thing the agency can properly answer is a factual clarification (for example, whether a non-resident may transit a securely caged pet rat through the province), included only as a secondary, agency-appropriate touchpoint, not as the reform lever. On the species-not-domestication point, the fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus) is itself the wild brown rat, domesticated only in the 19th century, so a captive-bred Rattus rattus is the same case one species over: https://blonderoofrat.com/how-the-sewer-rat-became-the-fancy-rat/.

Where to send it (more than one channel helps):

  • Legislative Assembly of Alberta — Members of the Legislative Assembly directory (Find Your MLA / Member Contact list) (legislature) — official contact page
    The total ban is set in statute (Agricultural Pests Act) and regulation (AR 184/2001). Only the Legislature can amend it, so your own MLA is the correct first touchpoint. This official directory lists all 87 MLAs by name and constituency with individual contact pages and a downloadable contact list, letting you reach the representative who can raise or sponsor a change.
  • Legislative Assembly of Alberta — Find Your MLA by riding (Elections Alberta MLA search) (legislature) — official contact page
    Use this official Elections Alberta tool to identify exactly which MLA represents your address/riding before you write, so your letter reaches your own representative (constituent letters carry the most weight).
  • Alberta Agriculture and Irrigation — Rat Control Program inbox (factual clarification ONLY, not policy change) (executive / agency) — rats@gov.ab.ca
    Included only for a narrow factual question this office can legitimately answer — e.g., whether a non-resident may transit a securely caged pet Rattus through Alberta. Do NOT use this channel to request legalization: the rat-control program is correctly enforcing the statute and cannot amend it. (Phone: 310-FARM in Alberta / 403-742-7901 outside.)

A starting-point message — please put it in your own words; a short personal note carries far more weight than an identical form letter:

English
Subject: Please amend the Agricultural Pests Act to allow domesticated pet rats

Dear [MLA name / Member for [constituency]],

I am a constituent writing about Alberta's total ban on keeping pet rats. Under the Agricultural Pests Act and the Pest and Nuisance Control Regulation (AR 184/2001), the entire genus Rattus is a declared pest, so even a tame, captive-bred pet rat kept indoors is illegal.

I fully support Alberta's program against wild, invasive rats. But the current law makes no distinction between a wild rat and a domesticated companion animal that is captive-bred, hand-tame, housed in a secure escape-proof cage, kept entirely indoors, and never released. I am not claiming such a pet poses zero risk. I am asking the Legislature to weigh whether the limited, controllable risk of a securely caged, altered, indoor-only animal that cannot establish a wild population is outweighed by allowing Albertans the kind of companionship that cats and dogs, themselves non-native, are already permitted to provide. That balance is yours to strike, and Alberta's wild-rat eradication program would continue unchanged.

The fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus) is itself the wild brown rat, domesticated only in the 19th century, so a captive-bred pet rat is the same case as the cats and dogs Alberta already permits.

Because this is set in statute and regulation, only the Legislature can fix it; the rat-control office is simply applying the law. I respectfully ask you to support amending the Act and Regulation to create a narrow exemption for domesticated pet rats kept under reasonable conditions (secure caging, no outdoor release, single-sex or altered housing), while Alberta's wild-rat eradication continues unchanged.

Thank you for considering this. I would welcome your reply.

Sincerely,
[Your name]
[Your address / constituency]
[Your email]

Summary. Alaska is the most restrictive state in the nation for the roof rat — it's flatly PROHIBITED. Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States › California

Summary. California restricts ALL rodents as 'detrimental' wild animals (14 CCR §671), and CDFW never issues possession permits for pets — so a normal wild-type roof rat is effectively illegal to keep. BUT the rule exempts 'domesticated races of rats or mice (white or albino; trained, dancing or spinning, laboratory-reared)', and that exemption is written by phenotype/origin, not by species — it doesn't name Rattus norvegicus. So a white/albino, trained, or documented laboratory-reared Rattus rattus may qualify, while a wild-type one does not. Whether a domesticated roof-rat line qualifies is the open question we've put to CDFW.

Cross-checked against official government sources.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
National law also applies. These are the California-specific rules; United States’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where California is silent. See United States.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Restricted

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

California classifies every species of Order Rodentia as a 'detrimental' restricted wild animal (14 CCR §671; FGC §2118), and CDFW categorically refuses Restricted Species Permits for PET purposes (only research/exhibition/education). The one opening is the exemption for 'domesticated races of rats or mice (white or albino; trained, dancing or spinning, laboratory-reared)' (14 CCR §671(c)(2)(J)(1)(c)) — which is defined by phenotype/origin, NOT by species. A white/albino, trained, or documented laboratory-reared roof rat may qualify; a phenotypically wild-type (agouti/black) roof rat is presumed an illegal restricted pest. Wild-caught roof rats can never be kept (FGC §3005.5).

Sources: CA Code of Regulations, CA Fish & Game Code, CA Fish & Game Code, CA Dept of Fish & Wildlife

Breeding   Restricted

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-06

Breeding restricted rodents is prohibited without research/exhibition permits. If the animals meet the 'domesticated races' exemption, breeding is outside CDFW's wildlife jurisdiction — but local animal-control/zoning rules apply, and any retail sale is governed by the Pet Store Animal Care Act.

Sources: CA Code of Regulations, CA Fish & Game Code

Selling or giving away   Restricted

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

Selling restricted wild rodents is prohibited. Selling EXEMPT domesticated rats is legal but regulated by California's Pet Store Animal Care Act (HSC §122350–122361), which sets enclosure, space, enrichment, and veterinary-care standards for anyone selling vertebrate pets.

Sources: CA Health & Safety Code, CA Code of Regulations

Transport & import   Restricted

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

Importing/transporting a restricted rodent needs a permit + Certificate of Veterinary Inspection. An EXEMPT domesticated rat may cross state lines without a restricted-species permit, but every animal entering California is still subject to inspection at CDFA border stations (the roof rat is a top agricultural pest), so carry documentation that the animal is an exempt domestic race. International movement is restricted federally (USFWS Form 3-177 — see United States).

Sources: CA Code of Regulations, CA Dept of Food & Agriculture

Restrictions & responsibilities

If the roof rat does NOT meet the 'domesticated races' exemption, it is a restricted species and CDFW issues permits only for research/exhibition/education — NOT pets — so keeping/breeding it as a pet is effectively prohibited (and wild-caught roof rats can never be kept, FGC §3005.5). Restricted-facility permits carry steep application + inspection fees and an emergency action plan.
  • Determine whether your animal meets the white/albino/trained/laboratory-reared exemption
  • If exempt, no CDFW permit is needed; if not, pet possession is not permitted

Forms: CDFW Restricted Species Permits · Where: CDFW License & Revenue Branch, Special Permits Unit · Fees: Restricted-species permits are not issued for pets

Source: CA Code of Regulations, CA Dept of Fish & Wildlife

Retail sale of an exempt domestic rat must meet the Pet Store Animal Care Act (HSC §122350–122361): structurally sound enclosures, adequate space, enrichment, separation of sick animals, and veterinary care.

Source: CA Health & Safety Code

All animals entering California pass CDFA border protection stations. Even an exempt domesticated roof rat may be stopped because it resembles a detrimental pest — carry proof (e.g., laboratory/breeder provenance) of its exempt domestic status.

Where: CDFA border protection stations

Source: CA Dept of Food & Agriculture

Never release or relocate a roof rat: relocating trapped wildlife is illegal (14 CCR §465.5), and releasing a nonnative species is prohibited. Wild roof rats may only be controlled lethally, never tamed/kept.

Source: CA Code of Regulations

It appears you can't currently keep a roof rat as a pet in California. Please confirm with the official sources above before acting. If you'd like to see this change, you can contact your representatives and the responsible agencies, ask them to treat a domesticated Rattus rattus line fairly and tell us what you learn so we can help others.

Help change this

How to help in California

California treats every rodent species as a "detrimental" restricted wild animal under Title 14 of the California Code of Regulations, section 671 (and Fish & Game Code section 2118), and the Department of Fish and Wildlife (CDFW) does not issue possession permits for pets. A wild-type roof rat (Rattus rattus) is therefore effectively illegal to keep. The same animal, bred in captivity, can be as tame as the common pet "fancy rat" (Rattus norvegicus), which is kept freely in California. The fancy rat is itself the wild brown rat (Rattus norvegicus), domesticated in the 19th century; a captive-bred roof rat is the same case one species over. Section 671 contains an exemption for "domesticated races of rats or mice (white or albino; trained, dancing or spinning, laboratory-reared)." That exemption is written by phenotype and origin, not by species. It says "rats or mice"; it does not name Rattus norvegicus and does not exclude Rattus rattus. A white/albino, demonstrably tame/trained, or documented laboratory-reared roof rat arguably fits the text, while a phenotypically wild-type one is presumed an illegal restricted pest. Whether CDFW reads the exemption to reach a domesticated roof-rat line, or treats it as fancy-rats-only, is the unresolved question, and it determines whether this is fixed by a clarification or by a rule change.

The ask: Two-track ask. (1) Ask CDFW's License & Revenue Branch / Special Permits Unit, in writing, to confirm whether the section 671(c)(2)(J)(1)(c) exemption for "domesticated races of rats or mice (white or albino; trained, dancing or spinning, laboratory-reared)" applies to a captive-bred, tame, domesticated line of roof rat (Rattus rattus), since the exemption is written by phenotype/origin and names no species, and to explain how the Department operationally defines "trained" and "laboratory-reared." (2) If CDFW answers that section 671 as written does not reach a domesticated roof rat, that is a question of the rule's text, which only the California Fish and Game Commission can change. The next ask is then a formal FGC 1 petition (and supporting public comment) to amend section 671 to add domesticated Rattus rattus to the exemption, the same path used to seek removal of the domestic ferret. The relevant question is domestication, not the wild ancestry of the species. The dog descends from the wolf and the house cat from a wild felid, yet California treats both as domestic animals because of generations bred for tameness, not their wild ancestry. The permitted fancy rat is itself the wild brown rat (Rattus norvegicus), domesticated in the 19th century (https://blonderoofrat.com/how-the-sewer-rat-became-the-fancy-rat/); a captive-bred roof rat is domesticated in that same sense, one species over. The Department and the Commission are asked to weigh that question, not to reach a particular result.

Where the lever really is: This is both levers in sequence, and the order matters. First, it is plausibly a bureaucracy-reading problem (lever = the AGENCY): the exemption text in 14 CCR §671 is species-blind ("rats or mice"; no binomial; verified against the regulation), so a clarification or declaratory answer from CDFW could confirm a domesticated R. rattus already qualifies, with no rule change needed. Start by asking CDFW's License & Revenue Branch / Special Permits Unit for a written interpretation. There is a ceiling: if CDFW responds that §671 is meant to cover only fancy rats / lab-reared origin and a wild-type roof rat is excluded, the obstacle is the rule's text and the listing of all Rodentia as "detrimental," and CDFW cannot rewrite the regulation by email. The body that owns and can amend 14 CCR §671 is the California Fish and Game Commission (FGC), via its formal petition-for-regulation-change process (FGC 1 form) and the associated public-comment window, the same lever the domestic-ferret campaign uses. Appealing further to CDFW will not change a rule it is correctly applying; that step requires an FGC rulemaking petition. If the Commission concludes the blanket Rodentia restriction in Fish & Game Code §2118 ties its hands, the final backstop is the Legislature. The fancy rat already permitted in California is itself the wild brown rat (Rattus norvegicus), domesticated in the 19th century (https://blonderoofrat.com/how-the-sewer-rat-became-the-fancy-rat/), and a captive-bred R. rattus is domesticated in the same sense one species over. Net: agency first for a clarification that may already exist in the text; Commission rulemaking if the text genuinely excludes the species.

Where to send it (more than one channel helps):

  • California Department of Fish and Wildlife — License & Revenue Branch / Special Permits Unit (Restricted Species) (executive / agency) — LRB@wildlife.ca.gov
    The Department that interprets and administers 14 CCR §671 and issues (and declines) restricted-species permits. This is the correct first stop for a written clarification on whether the species-blind 'domesticated races of rats or mice' exemption already reaches a captive-bred, tame roof rat. Verified official contact page; verified branch email LRB@wildlife.ca.gov and lines (916) 928-5805 / (916) 928-5846.
  • California Fish and Game Commission — Petition for Regulation Change (FGC 1) / Submit Comments (public comment) — fgc@fgc.ca.gov
    The rulemaking body that actually owns 14 CCR §671 and is the ONLY entity that can amend the restricted-species list or its exemptions. If CDFW reads the rule as excluding domesticated roof rats, this is where a formal FGC 1 petition (and public comment) to add domesticated Rattus rattus to the exemption must go — the same channel used for the domestic-ferret effort. Verified official petition page and inbox fgc@fgc.ca.gov.
  • California State Legislature — Find Your Representatives (legislature) — official contact page
    Backstop lever. The blanket classification of all Rodentia as restricted traces to Fish & Game Code §2118 (statute). If the Commission concludes the statute prevents it from exempting the species by regulation, only the Legislature can change the underlying law — so contacting your own Assembly Member and Senator becomes the route. Official legislative find-your-rep tool.

A starting-point message — please put it in your own words; a short personal note carries far more weight than an identical form letter:

English
To the California Department of Fish and Wildlife, License & Revenue Branch / Special Permits Unit:

I am writing to request a written clarification about the restricted-species exemption in 14 CCR §671(c)(2)(J)(1)(c). The rule restricts all rodents but exempts "domesticated races of rats or mice (white or albino; trained, dancing or spinning, laboratory-reared)." That exemption is written by phenotype and origin. It says "rats or mice" and names no species.

My question is whether this exemption applies to a captive-bred, domesticated and tame line of roof rat (Rattus rattus) that is white/albino, trained, or laboratory-reared, the same way it applies to the common pet rat (Rattus norvegicus). Domestication is a matter of an animal's breeding history and temperament, not its species. The dog descends from the wolf and the house cat from a wild felid, yet both are recognized as domestic animals because of generations bred for tameness, not their wild ancestry. The permitted fancy rat is itself the wild brown rat (Rattus norvegicus), domesticated in the 19th century, and a captive-bred roof rat is domesticated in that same sense. These animals are captive-bred, hand-tame, kept strictly indoors as pets, and never released into the wild.

If the Department reads §671 as not reaching a domesticated R. rattus, please say so plainly, and please explain how the Department defines "trained" and "laboratory-reared" for this exemption. If a regulatory change is required, I intend to petition the Fish and Game Commission.

Thank you for your time and for a written reply.

Sincerely,
[Your name]
[Your city, California]
[Your email]

Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States › Florida

Summary. Florida is permissive to keep a pet roof rat — with one paid-sale catch, now confirmed directly by FWC. FWC decides 'domestic vs. wild' by SPECIES, not by how tame an individual is, so roof/black rats count as 'wild rats' even when captive-bred for generations. The upshot (FWC Captive Wildlife, written reply 2026-06-08): KEEPING one as a pet needs NO license, and GIVING one away (any transfer with no money) needs NO license — all rats are exempt from personal-possession licensing. But SELLING one (any transfer for money) requires a Class III 'Exhibition or Public Sale' (ESC) license. Importing a roof rat into Florida needs a free 45-day FWC Wildlife Importation Permit plus a veterinary health certificate. Never release a nonnative.

Key points here are confirmed in writing by the responsible agency (see below).
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
National law also applies. These are the Florida-specific rules; United States’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where Florida is silent. See United States.
Confirmed by the agencies.
  • FWC Captive Wildlife Office (written reply, 2026-06-08): FWC determines whether an animal is domestic or wild by the SPECIES, not by an individual's tameness — so black/roof rats are treated as wild rats even when captive-bred. KEEPING one as a pet requires NO license (all rats, wild or domestic, are exempt from personal-possession licensing), and GIVING one away with no money changing hands requires NO license. SELLING one (any transfer for payment) requires a Class III 'Exhibition or Public Sale' (ESC) license.
  • FDACS Division of Animal Industry (written guidance, 2020): importing animals into Florida requires a veterinary health certificate (OCVI) issued within 30 days; reportable diseases must be reported.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-08

FWC confirmed in writing (2026-06-08) that ALL rats — wild or domestic — are exempt from personal-possession licensing, so keeping a captive-bred roof rat as a pet needs no FWC license. (Consistent with F.A.C. 68A-6.003(14)(d), which exempts 'Rats and mice' for personal use, and with roof rats not being on FWC's Prohibited Nonnative Species list.)

Sources: Florida Administrative Code, FL FWC

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-08

Breeding for personal use — keeping the offspring as your own pets or giving them away free — requires no FWC license (all rats are exempt from personal-possession licensing). There is no separate FWC 'breeding permit.' Note: the moment you SELL offspring (transfer for money), the selling rule below applies (a Class III ESC license).

Sources: Florida Administrative Code

Selling or giving away   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-08

RESOLVED by FWC's written reply (2026-06-08): because FWC treats roof rats as WILDLIFE by species (not by tameness), SELLING one — any transfer where money changes hands — requires a Class III 'Exhibition or Public Sale' (ESC) license. GIVING one away with no payment requires NO license (all rats are exempt from personal-possession licensing). This supersedes the brief 2020 verbal 'no license to sell' guidance, which didn't account for the species-based doctrine.

Sources: FL FWC, Florida Administrative Code, Florida Administrative Code

Transport & import   Restricted

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

Moving an exempt personal pet within Florida needs no permit. IMPORTING a roof rat into Florida (it is non-native wildlife) requires a FREE FWC Wildlife Importation Permit (CWL), valid 45 days (applicant must be 16+); and FDACS requires a veterinary health certificate (OCVI) for animals entering the state. It is illegal to release any nonnative species.

Sources: FL FWC, FDACS, FL FWC

Restrictions & responsibilities

To SELL roof rats (any transfer for money), you need a Class III 'License to Possess Wildlife for Exhibition or Public Sale' (ESC), $50/yr — confirmed required by FWC (2026-06-08) because roof rats are wildlife by species. GIVING them away free needs no license. No experience hours, but a disaster plan + inventory/source recordkeeping are required for the ESC.
  • If you'll sell for money: apply for the Class III Exhibition/Public Sale (ESC) license and file a disaster plan
  • If only giving away free: nothing required

Forms: FWC — Sale of Wildlife · Where: FWC Captive Wildlife Office · Fees: $50/yr (Class III ESC) to sell; $0 to give away

Source: FL FWC, Florida Administrative Code

To bring a roof rat INTO Florida, get a free FWC Wildlife Importation Permit (CWL), valid 45 days (applicant must be 16+), plus a veterinary health certificate (OCVI) issued within 30 days. Applies to private and commercial moves alike.
  • Apply for the FWC Wildlife Importation Permit (CWL) before crossing into Florida
  • Carry a veterinary health certificate (OCVI) issued within 30 days

Forms: FWC — Importation of Wildlife · Where: FWC Captive Wildlife Office · Fees: No cost (CWL); veterinary fee for the OCVI

Source: FL FWC, FDACS

It is illegal to release any nonnative species, including roof rats, into the wild in Florida. Keep them contained and rehome responsibly; never release. Local city/county ordinances may also limit exotic-pet keeping or large breeding operations.

Where: Your county animal services / municipal code enforcement

Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States › Massachusetts

Summary. Massachusetts is a strict 'prohibited-unless-listed' state — and the roof rat is NOT on the list. Its exemption list (321 CMR 9.01) and domestic-animals list (321 CMR 9.02) name only the Norway rat (Rattus norvegicus) and its laboratory strains — Rattus rattus appears nowhere. So a roof rat is treated as a non-listed undomesticated mammal that may not be kept without a MassWildlife permit, and MassWildlife states it 'will not be issued a permit for keeping a wild animal as a pet.' The result: keeping, breeding, selling, and importing a roof rat are effectively prohibited here — purely because the species isn't named, while its near-twin the fancy rat is. A textbook 'species-not-domestication' gap and a prime advocacy target.

Key points here are confirmed in writing by the responsible agency (see below).
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
National law also applies. These are the Massachusetts-specific rules; United States’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where Massachusetts is silent. See United States.
Confirmed by the agencies.
  • Massachusetts Division of Fisheries & Wildlife (MassWildlife), written reply June 2026: confirmed that roof rats (Rattus rattus) are not a legal pet in Massachusetts, and directed us to the state's published 'Wildlife as pets' guidance. This confirms there is no general pet-keeping pathway for R. rattus in Massachusetts — even though its near-twin the fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus) is exempt and fully legal. The barrier is that the species is simply absent from the state's exemption list, not a finding that domesticated roof rats are dangerous.
  • Massachusetts Division of Fisheries & Wildlife (MassWildlife), follow-up reply June 2026: confirmed that an educator may apply for a permit to possess roof rats, and provided the possession/importation application form. So while roof rats are not a general legal pet in Massachusetts, a documented educational or scientific keeper can apply to MassWildlife for a possession permit.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Restricted

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

R. rattus is not on the 321 CMR 9.01 exemption list nor the 321 CMR 9.02 domestic-animals list (both name only the Norway rat / laboratory rat derived from R. norvegicus). As a non-listed undomesticated mammal it may not be possessed without a MassWildlife license under M.G.L. c.131 §23 — and MassWildlife's own guidance states no permit is issued for keeping a wild animal as a pet, so there is no lawful pet pathway. Refined (assume-a-pathway re-audit): R. rattus isn't on the 321 CMR 9.01(12) exempt list (only R. norvegicus is), so possession needs a MassWildlife license under MGL c.131 §23 / 321 CMR 2.12 — BUT 2.12 requires DENIAL of applications to keep a wild animal 'as a pet' (MassWildlife: 'you will not be issued a permit for keeping a wild animal as a pet'). No private pet pathway; only a scientific/educational/commercial-propagator license (institutional). = restricted, not flat-prohibited. The operative trigger confirmed by Gemini DR (2026-06-10) is 321 CMR 9.02(2)(c): any vertebrate taxon not listed 'shall be presumed to be wild and shall be subject to the provisions of M.G.L. c. 131,' which is what subjects an unlisted R. rattus to the §23 licensing regime.

Sources: MA Division of Fisheries & Wildlife (via Cornell LII), MA Division of Fisheries & Wildlife (via Cornell LII), Massachusetts General Court, MA Division of Fisheries & Wildlife, MA Division of Fisheries & Wildlife (via Cornell LII)

Breeding   Restricted

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

Breeding an unlisted wild mammal requires a Class 4 Propagator's License under M.G.L. c.131 §23 / 321 CMR 2.12, which authorizes a holder to possess, maintain, propagate, buy, sell, or dispose of specified mammals — but acquisition is gated by an exhaustive application (scale diagrams/photos of enclosures, a written disposition plan and justification, documentary proof of professional husbandry qualifications, and a liability/inspection agreement). Critically, 321 CMR 2.12(9) MANDATES denial of any application to 'possess, maintain, propagate, or cultivate animals as pets,' or where the intent is 'purely on curiosity, impulse, novelty, or to provide personal amusement or entertainment.' There is therefore no hobby/small-breeder threshold: a Class 4 license for R. rattus is only structurally available for a certified non-pet purpose — scientific (recognized institution), educational (recognized institution), or commercial propagation for the agricultural/laboratory supply chain divorced from the pet trade. R. norvegicus needs none of this because it is exempt/domestic. Hobby/pet breeding is barred.

Sources: Massachusetts General Court, MA Division of Fisheries & Wildlife (via Cornell LII), MA Division of Fisheries & Wildlife (via Cornell LII), MA Division of Fisheries & Wildlife (via Cornell LII)

Selling or giving away   Restricted

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

Commercial sale, offer for sale, barter, or transfer of a presumed-wild mammal requires a Class 6 Dealer's License or a Class 4 Propagator's License under 321 CMR 2.12(3) / M.G.L. c.131 §23. Because R. rattus is unlisted, the 'without a permit' privilege in 321 CMR 9.01 does not reach it. A second, independent barrier blocks the retail pet channel: under 330 CMR 12.00 (Licensing and Operation of Pet Shops), a licensed pet shop may sell only an 'Animal,' defined as a species that may be kept without a MassWildlife permit per 321 CMR 9.01/9.02 — so the roof rat falls outside what any pet shop may lawfully sell. The result is a closed regulatory loop: a Class 4/Class 6 holder may transfer R. rattus only to another permitted person or institution, permanently sequestering the species from public pet ownership. Private give-away/sale of a pet roof rat is not authorized; only a licensed non-pet dealer/propagator transfer is structurally possible.

Sources: Massachusetts General Court, MA Division of Fisheries & Wildlife (via Cornell LII), MA Division of Fisheries & Wildlife (via Cornell LII), MA Dept of Agricultural Resources (via Animal Legal & Historical Center)

Transport & import   Restricted

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

Cross-border movement of R. rattus is treated as importation of 'wildlife' under 321 CMR 2.15 regardless of captive-bred origin. No person may import a live mammal without an Importation Permit from the Director (321 CMR 2.15(2)); the application must be filed at least ten days in advance with the originating/destination facility details and a signed certification that the export is lawful in the origin jurisdiction, and the Director may deny under 321 CMR 2.15(10) where importation is 'detrimental to the fish and wildlife resources of Massachusetts... and is not in the public interest' (a real risk given the roof rat's invasive-pest reputation), and may require zoonotic-disease/parasite health certificates; illegal or diseased imports may be seized and humanely destroyed (321 CMR 2.15(22)). Once lawfully in-state under permit, transport is allowed only with the permit accompanying the animal and subject to Director-imposed caging/safety conditions. Liberation is ABSOLUTELY barred — never release; release of a non-native presumed-wild rodent is a serious violation. So transport is permit-gated and restricted, not unregulated. (The MDAR animal-health/CVI layer is secondary to the wildlife-import permit.)

Sources: Massachusetts General Court, MA Division of Fisheries & Wildlife (via Cornell LII), MA Division of Fisheries & Wildlife (via Cornell LII), MA Dept of Agricultural Resources (via Cornell LII)

Restrictions & responsibilities

Because R. rattus is not on the Massachusetts exempt/domestic lists, there is no lawful way to keep it as a pet here — MassWildlife does not issue pet-keeping permits for wildlife. If you have a roof rat and move to Massachusetts, you cannot bring it; rehome it responsibly first. (The fancy rat, R. norvegicus, IS exempt and legal.)
  • Do not bring a roof rat into Massachusetts
  • If advocating: petition MassWildlife to add captive-bred R. rattus to the 321 CMR 9.02 / 9.01 lists

Where: Massachusetts Division of Fisheries & Wildlife (MassWildlife)

Source: MA Division of Fisheries & Wildlife, MA Division of Fisheries & Wildlife (via Cornell LII)

It appears you can't currently keep a roof rat as a pet in Massachusetts. Please confirm with the official sources above before acting. If you'd like to see this change, you can contact your representatives and the responsible agencies, ask them to treat a domesticated Rattus rattus line fairly and tell us what you learn so we can help others.

Help change this

How to help in Massachusetts

Massachusetts uses a "prohibited-unless-listed" system for keeping animals. The state's exemption list (321 CMR 9.01) and its domestic-animals list (321 CMR 9.02) name only the Norway rat (Rattus norvegicus) and the laboratory/fancy rat strains derived from it. The roof rat (Rattus rattus, also called the black rat) is not named on either list. The operative trigger is 321 CMR 9.02(2)(c): 'Any vertebrate taxa not listed in 321 CMR 9.02 shall be presumed to be wild and shall be subject to the provisions of M.G.L. c. 131.' The state therefore treats a roof rat as a non-listed wild mammal that cannot be kept without a MassWildlife license, and MassWildlife's guidance says it will not issue a permit to keep a wild animal as a pet. The practical result is that a tame, captive-bred roof rat is off-limits in Massachusetts because the species name is missing from a list, while its near-identical cousin the fancy rat is fully legal. This is a species-not-domestication gap, not a judgment that domesticated roof rats are dangerous or different to care for.

The ask: Ask MassWildlife to add captive-bred Rattus rattus to the 321 CMR 9.01 exemption list (subsection (12), List of Mammals) and/or the 321 CMR 9.02 domestic-animals list, the same regulatory route already used for the Norway rat / fancy rat. The controlling statute, M.G.L. c. 131 §23, lets the Director amend the list after a public hearing using four criteria. A domesticated, indoor-kept, captive-bred roof rat line appears to satisfy all four, and the Director is asked to weigh it against them: the roof rat is already established in the region, so an escaped tame animal adds little new ecological risk; it is no more dangerous or demanding to keep than the fancy rat the list already allows; and trade in a captive-bred line has little bearing on wild populations. The fancy rat is itself the wild brown rat (R. norvegicus), domesticated only in the 19th century (see https://blonderoofrat.com/how-the-sewer-rat-became-the-fancy-rat/), so a captive-bred R. rattus is the same case one species over. Whether the four criteria are met is the Director's judgment after a public hearing; the request is only that the question be evaluated. This can be raised informally by email, or formally as a petition for rulemaking under G.L. c. 30A §4 directed to the Director of the Division of Fisheries & Wildlife and the Fisheries and Wildlife Board (Permit Section, 100 Cambridge Street, 6th Floor, Boston, MA 02114).

Where the lever really is: This is an agency lever, not a legislative one. The barrier is a regulation the agency itself writes and controls: the exemption list lives in 321 CMR 9.01, a MassWildlife regulation, and the enabling statute M.G.L. c. 131 §23 authorizes the Director of the Division of Fisheries & Wildlife to alter that list after a public hearing, applying four statutory criteria (no ecological harm from escape, no danger to people, care no harder than a common domestic animal, no impact on wild populations). The roof rat's absence is a gap: the species was never added. The agency has both the power and a built-in mechanism to fix it. The Norway rat / fancy rat got onto the list the same way, and sugar gliders, the four-toed hedgehog, and several chameleons and skinks were all later added to 321 CMR 9.01 through this process. The right move is to ask MassWildlife to add captive-bred R. rattus, either informally by writing to the Division or formally by filing a petition for rulemaking under the Massachusetts Administrative Procedure Act (G.L. c. 30A §4), which gives any interested person the right to ask an agency to amend a regulation and obliges the agency to consider it. The procedural path after a meritorious petition is: agency scientific review, then a public hearing noticed at least 21 days in advance in the Massachusetts Register, then a written comment period, then a Small Business Impact Statement, then a Fisheries and Wildlife Board vote, then final promulgation with the Secretary of the Commonwealth. A legislative bill is not the primary path here, because no statute names or bans the roof rat; the gap is administrative. If the species had been written into a statute by name, appealing to the agency would be pointless and the legislature would be needed, but that is not the situation in Massachusetts.

Where to send it (more than one channel helps):

  • Massachusetts Division of Fisheries & Wildlife (MassWildlife) (executive / agency) — Mass.Wildlife@mass.gov
    MassWildlife writes and maintains the 321 CMR 9.01 exemption list and the 9.02 domestic-animals list, and under M.G.L. c. 131 §23 its Director can add a species to that list after a public hearing. This is the office with the actual power to fix the gap. Mass.Wildlife@mass.gov is the agency's official general inbox (verified on mass.gov); start here to ask for clarification and to request that captive-bred Rattus rattus be added, the same way Rattus norvegicus already is.
  • MassWildlife — formal Petition for Rulemaking under G.L. c. 30A §4 (public comment) — Mass.Wildlife@mass.gov
    If an informal request stalls, the Massachusetts Administrative Procedure Act (G.L. c. 30A §4) gives any interested person the right to file a written petition asking an agency to amend a regulation, and the agency must consider it. A petition to add captive-bred R. rattus to 321 CMR 9.01(12) forces the Division to formally consider the request and respond, and any list change triggers the public hearing required by M.G.L. c. 131 §23 — your chance to make the case on the record. Route the written petition to the Director of the Division of Fisheries & Wildlife and the Fisheries and Wildlife Board via the Permit Section, MassWildlife, 100 Cambridge Street, 6th Floor, Boston, MA 02114 (and copy the official Mass.Wildlife@mass.gov inbox). Board communications can also be addressed to the Chairman, Fisheries and Wildlife Board, 1 Rabbit Hill Road, Westborough, MA 01581.

A starting-point message — please put it in your own words; a short personal note carries far more weight than an identical form letter:

English
To the Massachusetts Division of Fisheries & Wildlife (Director and Permit Section),

I am writing about a gap in the exemption list at 321 CMR 9.01. That list, and the domestic-animals list at 321 CMR 9.02, name the Norway rat (Rattus norvegicus) and its laboratory and fancy strains, but they do not name the roof rat (Rattus rattus, the black rat). Under 321 CMR 9.02(2)(c) any taxon not listed 'shall be presumed to be wild,' so because of that omission a tame, captive-bred roof rat cannot be kept in Massachusetts, even though its near-identical cousin the fancy rat is fully legal.

These are domesticated, captive-bred animals: selectively bred for tameness, kept entirely indoors as pets, and never released. They are not wild-caught and are no more demanding to care for than any common pet rodent.

I respectfully ask the Division to add captive-bred Rattus rattus to the 321 CMR 9.01 exemption list (subsection (12), List of Mammals) and/or the 9.02 domestic-animals list, the same route already used for the Norway rat and, more recently, for sugar gliders, the four-toed hedgehog, and several chameleons and skinks. Under M.G.L. c. 131 §23, a captive-bred domestic line appears to meet all four statutory criteria: (1) accidental release is unlikely to adversely affect the ecology of the Commonwealth, because the roof rat is already established in the region and a tame, captive-bred animal is poorly suited to surviving unaided; (2) the animal in captivity or escaped poses little danger to people by injury or disease; (3) its care is no more demanding in any major respect than common domestic animals; and (4) trade in a captive-bred line is unlikely to significantly affect wild populations. Whether these criteria are met is the Director's determination after a public hearing. I am asking that the question be evaluated, not assuming its outcome.

Please tell me the administrative procedure, designated recipient, and expected timeline for docketing such a request, and whether I should submit it as a formal petition for rulemaking under G.L. c. 30A §4 for a Fisheries and Wildlife Board hearing. I would also welcome the Division's view on whether the presumption of wildness under 321 CMR 9.02(2)(c) is rebuttable on a showing of domestication, or whether a full rulemaking is the only remedy. Thank you for your time.

Sincerely,
[Your name]
[Your town]
[Your email]

Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States › New York

Summary. Keeping, breeding, and selling pet roof rats is legal in New York — both statewide and in New York City. The state classifies Rattus rattus as 'unprotected wildlife,' which may be possessed and sold without restriction (ECL §11-0917(2)); it is not a prohibited 'wild animal' and not on the invasive-species list. NYC's Health Code bans only 'large rodents,' so small pet rats are allowed (a Class P pet-shop permit is needed only for commercial retail). Bringing a rat into NY from another state needs a 30-day vet health certificate; international movement is federally restricted.

Cross-checked against official government sources.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
National law also applies. These are the New York-specific rules; United States’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where New York is silent. See United States.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

New York classifies Rattus rattus as 'unprotected wildlife,' which ECL §11-0917(2) says 'may be possessed, transported, bought and sold without restriction.' It is not a prohibited 'wild animal' (ECL §11-0512 / §11-0103(6)(e) lists primates, big cats, canids, bears, venomous reptiles, crocodilians — not rodents) and is not on the state invasive-species list (6 NYCRR Part 575). New York CITY allows it too: the NYC Health Code (Art. 161.01(b)(14)) bans only 'large rodents' (beaver, capybara, prairie dog, porcupine, etc.); small domestic rats are permitted.

Sources: NY State Senate (Consolidated Laws), NY State Senate, NYC DOHMH

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

No New York breeder license for rodents — the 'Pet Dealer' law (Agriculture & Markets Law Art. 26-A, §400) defines 'animal' as only dogs and cats, so breeding rats at any volume is outside it; only the general anti-cruelty rules apply. In NYC, hobby breeding is fine, but sanitation/nuisance rules (odor, escapes) apply.

Sources: NY Consolidated Laws

Selling or giving away   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

Statewide, selling roof rats is legal — a retailer must just give buyers written/digital care instructions for 'small animals' (which the law lists as including rats), per General Business Law §391-t. In New York CITY, a commercial retail seller needs a Class P 'Pet Shop' permit (NYCHC §161.09); NYC's Local Law 132 (2024) banned the retail sale of dogs, cats, guinea pigs and rabbits, but rats remain sellable. Giving rats away or private/face-to-face placement needs no permit. (Federal USDA licensing applies to wholesale/sight-unseen sales — see United States.)

Sources: NY State Senate, NYC DOHMH

Transport & import   Restricted

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-06

Within New York, no permit is required. Bringing a rat INTO New York from another state requires a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (health certificate) issued within 30 days (1CRR-NY 67.2); no rabies vaccine is required for rodents, and enforcement against a private owner with a single pet is reportedly minimal. International import/export is restricted at the federal level (USFWS Form 3-177; CDC African-rodent ban) — see United States.

Sources: NY Dept. of Agriculture & Markets

Restrictions & responsibilities

In New York CITY, a commercial retail seller of rats needs a Class P 'Pet Shop' permit from DOHMH (facility inspections; integrated pest management). Rats remain legally sellable in NYC even after Local Law 132 (2024) banned retail sale of dogs/cats/guinea pigs/rabbits. Private/face-to-face placement and giveaways need no permit.
  • If running an NYC retail storefront, obtain a DOHMH Class P pet-shop permit

Forms: NYC Health Code Ch. 5 — Pet Shops · Where: NYC DOHMH · Fees: Municipal pet-shop permit fee

Source: NYC DOHMH

Statewide, a retailer selling rats must give the buyer written or digital care instructions for the species at the time of sale (GBS §391-t), and keep copies on file.

Source: NY State Senate

Bringing a rat into New York from another state requires a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (CVI) issued within 30 days by a USDA-accredited vet (1CRR-NY 67.2). No rabies vaccine is required for rodents.
  • Have a USDA-accredited vet issue a CVI within 30 days of entry

Forms: NY Companion Animal Import & Export · Where: Carried with the animal · Fees: Veterinary fee

Source: NY Dept. of Agriculture & Markets

Keep rats in escape-proof caging — an escaped pet rat is legally indistinguishable from a feral pest under NYC's rodent-control rules (Art. 151), and harborage/active-rodent-signs carry fines. Never release a nonnative species.

Source: NYC DOHMH

Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States › Texas

Summary. Texas does not regulate keeping, breeding, or selling pet roof rats at the state level, now confirmed in writing by TPWD (June 2026): as a non-native exotic rodent, Rattus rattus falls outside TPWD's 'nongame' wildlife rules (indigenous species only), the 'dangerous wild animal' law, and TAHC's 'exotic livestock' (hooved-animal) entry rules. A retail storefront still needs the local city's pet-shop license, wholesale/sight-unseen sales trigger federal USDA licensing, and international movement is federally restricted (roof rats are 'wildlife'). Releasing one is illegal.

Key points here are confirmed in writing by the responsible agency (see below).
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
National law also applies. These are the Texas-specific rules; United States’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where Texas is silent. See United States.
Confirmed by the agencies.
  • Texas Parks & Wildlife Department (Wildlife Permits Office), written reply June 2026: because roof rats (Rattus rattus) are not native to Texas, no TPWD permit is required to keep them. All TPWD permits regulate the possession, transport, and display of native/indigenous species only, so a non-native roof rat is entirely outside TPWD's permit scope.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

Texas regulates exotic-pet possession by banning specific hazardous species, not by a permit list. Rattus rattus is a non-native rodent, so it is outside TPWD's 'nongame' wildlife rules (which cover only species INDIGENOUS to Texas, TPWC §67.001) and is not a listed 'dangerous wild animal' (Health & Safety Code ch. 822). No state possession permit is required. (Local ordinances may cap how many pets a household may keep.)

Sources: Texas Statutes, Texas Statutes

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

There is no Texas breeder license for rodents — the Dog or Cat Breeders Act (Occupations Code ch. 802) covers only dogs and cats. Hobby and commercial rat breeding are unregulated by the state. (Federal USDA licensing still applies to WHOLESALE or sight-unseen sales — see United States.)

Sources: Texas Statutes

Selling or giving away   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

Selling or giving roof rats is unregulated by the state: the TPWD Commercial Nongame Dealer permit applies only to INDIGENOUS wildlife (31 TAC §65.325), so it doesn't cover non-native rats. Two layers still apply: a retail storefront needs the local city's pet-shop license, and wholesale or sight-unseen sales trigger federal USDA licensing (see United States).

Sources: Texas Parks & Wildlife, Texas Statutes

Transport & import   Legal

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-06

Within Texas and across state lines, no state permit or health certificate is required for pet rats: rodents are exempt from TAHC's 'exotic livestock' entry rules (those cover hooved animals) and from the DSHS rabies transport ban (rodents are low-risk). Airlines typically require a vet health certificate to fly. International import/export is restricted at the FEDERAL level (USFWS Form 3-177; CDC African-rodent ban) — see United States.

Sources: TAHC, Texas DSHS

Restrictions & responsibilities

A retail pet-store storefront needs the local city's Pet Shop License / commercial animal establishment permit (sanitation, zoning, records). Rules vary by municipality (Houston, Austin, Dallas, etc.). Private/face-to-face placement and giveaways do not need a state license.
  • Check your city's animal-establishment / pet-shop licensing if running a storefront

Where: Your city's animal control / code enforcement · Fees: Set locally

Source: Texas Parks & Wildlife

Releasing or abandoning a roof rat is illegal in Texas — it is criminal abandonment under the animal-cruelty law (Penal Code §42.092), and they are an invasive non-native species. Rehome responsibly (shelter, rescue, or new owner); never release.

Source: Texas Statutes
